e: Segregation of duties splits key steps, such as setting up vendors, approving payments and recording them, among different people. One employee can't create a fake vendor and pay it, so fraud would require collusion. It's one of the most important internal controls.

q: Why does compliance matter so much in the finance industry?
o: It maintains public trust in the financial system
It guarantees every investment will make money
It replaces the need for internal audits
It lets firms avoid paying taxes
e: The financial system runs on trust: people deposit, invest and borrow only if they believe institutions follow the rules. Compliance with laws and regulations protects customers, keeps markets fair and keeps institutions stable, which maintains public trust. It can't guarantee returns.

q: A compliance review that finds problems after transactions have already happened, such as a monthly audit of wire transfers, is a(n)
e: Detective controls find problems that have already happened, such as audits, reconciliations and reviews of past transactions. Preventive controls stop problems before they occur, such as approvals and access limits. A monthly audit of past wire transfers is detective.

q: What is a main benefit of using technology for compliance work?
o: It completes monitoring faster and with fewer human errors
It removes all regulations a firm must follow
It eliminates the need for compliance staff entirely
It guarantees regulators will never audit the firm
e: Regulatory technology (RegTech) automates monitoring, screening and reporting, so compliance work is faster, cheaper and less error-prone, and it can review far more data than people could. Firms still must follow every regulation and keep compliance staff to make judgment calls.

q: A bank uses software that scans every transaction overnight and flags patterns that could signal money laundering. This is an example of
e: Automated transaction monitoring reviews every transaction against rules and patterns, such as structuring cash deposits just under $10,000, and flags suspicious activity for investigators. It covers 100% of transactions instead of a small manual sample.

q: Software that continuously reviews a firm's records and flags exceptions, so auditors don't have to check every document by hand, is sometimes called a
e: Automated audit tools, sometimes called virtual auditors, continuously test large volumes of records against rules and flag exceptions for humans to review. That's faster and more complete than checking documents by hand.

q: How does compliance technology usually affect a firm's costs over time?
o: It reduces costs by automating repetitive work
It raises costs because every task must be done twice
It has no effect on costs
e: Compliance technology has an upfront cost, but by automating repetitive tasks like screening, monitoring and report preparation, it lowers the ongoing cost of compliance and frees staff for complex work. It doesn't double work or affect only marketing costs.

q: Which use of data analytics helps a finance company stay compliant?
o: Identifying unusual patterns and trends in transactions
e: Data analytics can spot unusual patterns and trends in transactions, such as sudden spikes, odd timing or activity that doesn't fit a customer's profile, which may signal fraud or rule violations. Catching them early keeps the company compliant and limits losses.

q: Know-your-customer software that compares a customer's photo ID with a live selfie helps a bank
e: KYC rules require banks to verify customers' identities. Software that compares a photo ID with a live selfie, often using facial recognition and document checks, makes verification faster for honest customers and harder to fool with stolen or fake IDs.

q: Maria sold stock at a $2,000 loss this year and has $5,000 of gains on other stock. How can tax law help her?
o: She can use the loss to offset part of her gains
She must pay extra tax because of the loss
She can deduct the loss only if she buys the same stock the next day
Losses can never be used for taxes
e: Capital losses offset capital gains. Maria's $5,000 of gains minus her $2,000 loss leaves $3,000 of taxable net gains. Watch the wash-sale rule: buying the same or a substantially identical stock within 30 days before or after the sale disallows the loss.

q: Which accounts give tax advantages specifically to encourage saving for retirement and health costs?
e: Congress uses tax breaks to encourage saving: 401(k)s and IRAs (traditional or Roth) for retirement, and health savings accounts, which are triple tax-advantaged, for medical costs. Checking accounts, credit cards and car loans have no special tax treatment.

q: With a Roth IRA, contributions are made with after-tax money, so qualified withdrawals in retirement are
o: added to the next year's income
e: Because Roth IRA contributions are made with money you've already paid tax on, qualified withdrawals in retirement, including decades of growth, are tax-free. The trade-off is no deduction today. Roth makes the most sense when your tax rate now is lower than you expect later.

q: Before recommending any product, what should a financial advisor learn first?
o: The firm's sales targets for the month
Which product pays the highest commission
e: Every good recommendation starts with understanding the client: their goals, expectations, timeline and risk tolerance. Know-your-customer and best-interest rules require it. Sales targets, commissions or favorite brands shouldn't drive advice.

q: An advisor would earn a bonus for selling one fund over another. To act responsibly, the advisor should first
o: disclose the conflict of interest to the client
hide the bonus to avoid confusing the client
refuse to work with the client
e: A bonus tied to one fund is a conflict of interest, because the advisor's personal gain could sway the recommendation. The advisor must disclose it to the client and still recommend what's truly best for them. Hiding it is a breach of trust and of best-interest rules.

q: A CRM system's biggest advantage for a finance team is that it
o: keeps all customer data in one hub for organizing and analysis
replaces the need to talk with customers
e: A CRM keeps all customer data, including contact details, accounts, goals and every interaction, in one central hub that the whole team can use. That consistency means any team member can give informed, personal service. It supports conversations with customers; it doesn't replace them.

q: Finding and fixing outdated, duplicate or wrong customer records in a CRM database is called
e: Data cleansing finds and corrects inaccurate, outdated or duplicate records, like a client listed twice or an old address. Clean data makes CRM reports, analytics and personalized messages accurate. Data mining finds patterns in data; it doesn't fix it.

q: A bank uses its CRM to estimate how much revenue a customer will bring in over the whole relationship. This measure is
e: Customer lifetime value (CLV) estimates the total revenue or profit a customer will bring over the whole relationship. A customer likely to have a mortgage, cards and investments for 20 years is worth investing in, which guides how much to spend on service and retention.

q: Records of every call, email, meeting and website visit with a customer, stored in a CRM, are
e: Interaction data records how and when customers engage with the firm through calls, emails, meetings and website visits. It shows what customers care about and how they prefer to communicate, which helps personalize service. Demographic data is age, income and location.

q: An advisor uses CRM data to send a client a note about 529 plans the week the client's baby is born. This shows how CRM helps firms
e: CRM data about life events, like a new baby, lets firms send timely, relevant, personalized messages such as information on 529 college savings plans. Personal, well-timed communication builds loyalty and helps the client, without lowering prices or avoiding regulations.

q: CRM analytics that spot customers likely to need a mortgage soon help a bank identify
e: When analytics flag customers likely to need a product soon, such as a mortgage for renters with rising savings, the bank has identified sales opportunities. Reaching out with the right offer at the right time helps the customer and grows the business.

q: Banks, credit unions and savings institutions are called financial intermediaries because they
o: channel money from savers to borrowers
e: Financial intermediaries stand between savers and borrowers: they collect deposits from people with extra money and lend it to people and businesses who need it. That makes saving and borrowing easier and safer for both. The Treasury and Fed handle currency, and Congress sets taxes.

q: Commodities such as coffee, sugar and cotton, which are grown rather than mined, are known as
e: Soft commodities are agricultural products that are grown, such as coffee, sugar, cotton, cocoa and wheat. Hard commodities are mined or extracted, such as gold, oil and copper. Both trade in commodities markets, often through futures contracts.

q: When a bank, an insurance company and a brokerage combine their services so customers can bank, insure and invest in one place, the industry trend is called
e: Convergence is the blurring of lines between types of financial firms, so one company offers banking, insurance and investing in one place. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 made it legal. Deregulation is removing rules, and disintermediation is bypassing intermediaries.

q: The sale of insurance products through a bank's branches and customer relationships is known as
e: Bancassurance (bank + assurance) is when a bank sells insurance through its branches and to its existing customers. It's a form of convergence: the bank earns fees, and the insurer reaches customers who already trust the bank.

q: When two companies merge and both original companies cease to exist, forming a brand-new legal entity, this is a
e: In a consolidation, both original companies cease to exist and a brand-new legal entity is formed (A + B = C). In a statutory merger, one company absorbs the other and survives (A + B = A). Both reduce the number of firms in an industry.

q: A major reason financial firms consolidate is to
o: lower costs through economies of scale
e: Economies of scale mean the cost per customer falls as a firm grows. Technology, cybersecurity, compliance and headquarters costs are largely fixed, so spreading them over more customers lowers costs. Consolidation reduces the number of competitors, not increases it.

q: During an economic contraction, stocks in which sector tend to hold up best because people need them regardless of the economy?
e: Health care is a defensive sector: people still need medicine, doctors and hospitals in a recession, so sales and earnings stay relatively steady. Luxury travel, new homes and high-end jewelry are cyclical; people cut back on them when money is tight.

q: Stock prices often start falling before a recession officially begins. That makes the stock market a
e: A leading indicator changes before the overall economy does. Investors price stocks on expected future earnings, so the market often falls before a recession starts and rises before a recovery. Unemployment is a lagging indicator that changes after the economy turns.

q: When investors expect company profits to drop in the coming year, stock prices generally
e: A stock's price reflects what investors expect the company to earn in the future. If they expect profits to fall, they're willing to pay less for the shares, so prices generally fall, often before the lower profits are reported.

q: A country moving from an agriculture-based economy toward industry, with growing but volatile financial markets, is often called a(n)
e: An emerging market economy is industrializing and growing quickly, with developing financial markets, such as India, Brazil or Vietnam. Growth creates opportunity, but less mature markets and institutions make it more volatile than a mature economy like the U.S.

q: Over recent decades, most major economies shifted from exchange rates set by governments to rates set by supply and demand. This was a move from
e: Under fixed exchange rates, governments set and defend a currency's value; under floating rates, supply and demand in the currency market set it. Since the early 1970s, when the Bretton Woods system ended, most major currencies have floated, so their values change daily.

q: What is a key challenge when comparing companies from different countries?
o: Financial reporting requirements vary by country
All countries use exactly the same accounting rules
Foreign companies don't issue financial statements
e: Countries have different accounting standards (U.S. GAAP versus IFRS) and different disclosure requirements, so the same transaction can be reported differently. That makes comparing a U.S. company with a foreign one harder and requires adjusting for the differences.

q: Investing in a country whose stock market is unstable because it's moving from a government-controlled to a market economy carries extra
e: A transitional economy moving from government control to a market system often has unstable markets, changing laws, political uncertainty and currency swings. Those factors add investment risk, even though growth can be high. Foreign stocks have no FDIC protection or guaranteed return.

q: Which document gives shareholders a company's audited financial statements, a letter from management and a review of the year?
e: The annual report gives shareholders the audited financial statements, a letter from management and a review of the year's performance and strategy. Public companies also file the more detailed 10-K with the SEC. A securities table shows only trading data.

q: A public company must file a Form 8-K with the SEC to
o: report a major event, such as a CEO resignation or a merger
e: Form 8-K is the SEC's 'current report' for significant unscheduled events, such as an executive leaving, a merger, a bankruptcy or a major contract, generally due within four business days. It keeps investors informed between quarterly 10-Qs and annual 10-Ks.

q: Which financial statement shows what a company owns and owes on a specific date, which investors use to judge its financial strength?
e: The balance sheet lists assets (what the company owns), liabilities (what it owes) and shareholders' equity at a specific date. Investors use it to judge financial strength: liquidity, debt levels and the owners' stake. The income statement shows profit over a period.

q: An investor wants independent ratings and research on mutual funds and stocks. Which source is best known for this?
e: Morningstar is an independent investment research firm best known for its star ratings and analysis of mutual funds, ETFs and stocks. The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy, the IRS collects taxes and FINRA BrokerCheck shows brokers' backgrounds, not investment ratings.

q: Where on a public company's website would an investor most likely find earnings releases, SEC filings and presentations?
e: The investor relations section of a public company's website collects information for shareholders: earnings releases, SEC filings, annual reports, presentations and webcast replays. Careers pages, product catalogs and support chats serve job seekers and customers.

q: Compared with 30 years ago, finding information about a stock today is
o: easier than ever, because of free online data and filings
e: Free resources such as SEC EDGAR, company investor relations sites, financial news and brokerage apps make stock information available to anyone instantly. Thirty years ago, investors relied on newspapers, brokers and mailed reports. Today the challenge is filtering good information from hype.

q: A stock table shows: Last 41.80, Net Chg +0.45. What was the previous day's closing price?
e: Net change shows how much today's price moved from the previous day's close. If the stock is at $41.80 after rising $0.45, yesterday's close was $41.80 - $0.45 = $41.35. Adding instead of subtracting ($42.25) is the common trap.

q: A stock pays an annual dividend of $1.50 and trades at $50. What is its dividend yield?
e: Dividend yield = annual dividend per share / share price = $1.50 / $50 = 0.03, or 3%. It shows the income return on the investment, like an interest rate. If the price rose to $60 with the same dividend, the yield would fall to 2.5%.

q: In a stock table, the dividend column is blank for a company. This most likely means the company
o: pays the highest dividend in its industry
e: A blank dividend column means the company doesn't currently pay a regular dividend. Many growth companies reinvest all profits to expand instead. It doesn't mean the company is bankrupt or unlisted; it's listed in the table because it trades publicly.

q: A stock's price swings widely from day to day compared with the overall market. Investors describe this as high
e: Volatility measures how much and how quickly a price moves up and down. A stock that swings widely compared with the market has high volatility, which means more risk and more uncertainty about its value when you need to sell. Liquidity is how easily it can be traded.

q: A lender reviews an applicant's income, debt-to-income ratio and credit rating mainly to
o: judge how likely the applicant is to repay
e: Income shows the ability to make payments, debt-to-income shows how much of that income is already committed, and the credit rating shows the track record of repaying. Together they help the lender judge how likely the applicant is to repay, which drives the approval and the rate.

q: Which ratio measures a company's ability to pay current liabilities using only its most liquid assets (excluding inventory)?
e: The acid-test (quick) ratio = (cash + marketable securities + accounts receivable) / current liabilities. It excludes inventory, which may be slow to sell, so it's a stricter test of short-term liquidity than the current ratio. Around 1.0 or higher is generally healthy.

q: Expressing each line of a customer's income statement as a percentage of total revenue is
e: Vertical (common-size) analysis shows each line as a percentage of a base, here total revenue, within a single period. It reveals cost structure, like COGS at 60% of sales, and allows comparison across companies of different sizes. Horizontal analysis compares the same item across periods.

q: A main purpose of the financial-information management function is to
o: guide decision-making with accurate financial data
e: Financial-information management gathers, processes and reports accurate financial data so managers can make sound decisions about budgets, pricing, investment and cost control. Product design, hiring and competitors' prices aren't part of its role.

q: A company's financial-information system tracks how long customers take to pay. This helps the company
e: An aging report groups accounts receivable by how long they've been unpaid (0-30, 31-60, 61-90 and 90+ days). It shows which customers are overdue so the company can follow up, adjust credit terms and protect cash flow.

q: Financial-information management can support operations managers by
o: analyzing past resource usage to plan future needs
e: Historical data on how much material, labor and equipment time was used helps operations managers forecast future needs, plan purchasing and schedule staff. Financial information supports operational decisions, not just accounting reports.

q: A challenge for many companies is that financial data are stored in separate, task-specific software. This makes the data
e: When financial data sits in separate, task-specific programs (data silos), it's hard to access, combine and analyze, and numbers may not match across systems. Integrated systems like enterprise resource planning (ERP) solve this by putting data in one place.

q: Treating company financial data as something you must protect and use responsibly on behalf of others is known as
e: Stewardship means managing resources that belong to others, here financial data, responsibly, accurately and securely. A good data steward protects confidentiality, ensures accuracy and uses data only for proper purposes. Speculation, leverage and arbitrage are investing terms.

q: A record that shows who entered or changed each financial transaction, and when, is called a(n)
e: An audit trail records who entered or changed each transaction, what changed and when. It makes records traceable, which supports accountability and helps auditors detect errors or tampering. A trial balance lists account balances to check that debits equal credits.

q: An analyst learns that a company she's reviewing is owned by her brother. The ethical response is to
o: disclose the relationship and step away from the assignment
finish the review quickly without telling anyone
give the company a better rating
ask her brother for inside information
e: Reviewing a company owned by her brother is a conflict of interest that could bias her judgment or appear to. The ethical response is to disclose the relationship and step away so someone impartial does the review. Keeping quiet, favoring the company or seeking inside information are serious breaches.

q: Enterprise resource planning (ERP) software helps a company by
o: linking accounting, inventory, payroll and other data in one system
e: ERP software, such as SAP or Oracle, links accounting, inventory, purchasing, payroll and other functions in one integrated system with shared, real-time data. That eliminates duplicate entry and data silos. It doesn't replace employees, budgets or guarantee profits.

q: Which technology protects a company's financial network by blocking unauthorized access?
e: Firewall software, or hardware, monitors network traffic and blocks unauthorized access based on security rules, forming a barrier between internal systems and the internet. Macros, cameras and presentation software don't protect networks.

q: Laws that recognize electronic records and signatures as legally binding have allowed companies to
o: store and sign financial documents digitally
e: The federal E-SIGN Act (2000) and the state Uniform Electronic Transactions Act made electronic signatures and records legally valid. That allowed companies to sign contracts, store records and send statements digitally, cutting paper and speeding transactions. Records still must be kept.

q: Automatically importing bank transactions into accounting software improves data accuracy because it
o: removes the need to reconcile ever
e: Bank feeds import transactions directly, so no one has to retype amounts, dates and payees. That removes typing mistakes and transposed digits. Reconciling the books against bank statements is still good practice to catch duplicates or miscategorized items.

q: A budget that combines the sales, production, expense, cash and capital budgets into one plan is the
e: The master budget is the company's complete financial plan, combining the operating budgets (sales, production, expenses), the cash budget and the capital budget, plus budgeted financial statements. Every other budget feeds into it.

q: What is the main weakness of a static budget?
o: It doesn't adjust for changes in activity levels
It is illegal for public companies
e: A static budget is built for one expected level of activity and doesn't change. If sales or production differ, comparisons are misleading: costs naturally rise with higher volume, so the budget can't tell good cost control from bad. A flexible budget adjusts to actual activity.

q: Budgeting software that lets managers build unlimited 'what if' scenarios helps them
o: see the likely impact of decisions before making them
e: Scenario ('what-if') modeling lets managers change assumptions, like sales, prices, costs or interest rates, and see the impact before deciding. Comparing best, expected and worst cases prepares the company for different outcomes. It can't eliminate risk or replace forecasting.

q: A company asks each department to build its own budget estimate, then combines them into the company budget. This is a
e: In bottom-up budgeting, each department estimates its own needs and the estimates are combined into the company budget. People closest to the work usually estimate more accurately and feel more committed to the numbers. Top-down budgeting is set by leaders and passed down.

q: Comparing a company's ratios with those of top competitors and industry averages is called
e: Benchmarking compares a company's performance measures, such as margins, costs and ratios, with competitors or industry averages. If a rival's profit margin is 12% and yours is 8%, benchmarking shows where to improve. Bootstrapping is self-funding, and factoring is selling receivables.

q: Comparing a company's revenue and expenses for 2024, 2025 and 2026 to spot trends is
e: Horizontal (trend) analysis compares the same line items across several periods, such as revenue in 2024, 2025 and 2026, to spot growth or decline. Vertical analysis compares items as percentages of a base within one period.

q: Investors analyze a company's financial statements before buying its stock mainly to
o: assess the risk and potential return of the investment
e: Financial statements show a company's profitability, debt, cash flow and stability. Investors analyze them to judge the risk and potential return of buying the stock: is the company growing, profitable and able to pay its debts? Employee addresses and taxes aren't the purpose.

q: A report that shows how a company's operations affect the environment and society, alongside financial results, is a
e: A sustainability report presents environmental and social results, such as emissions, energy and water use and workforce data, alongside financial results, showing long-term impact. A 10-Q is a quarterly financial report, and a bank reconciliation matches cash records.

q: Lean management uses financial information mainly to
e: Lean management aims to eliminate waste, meaning any activity, inventory or step that doesn't add value for the customer. Cost data shows where waste is most expensive, such as excess inventory or rework, so it can be removed. Adding inventory or steps would increase waste.

q: Activity-based costing gives a property company a more accurate view of each rental's profit because it
o: assigns overhead based on the activities each property actually uses
e: Activity-based costing traces overhead to the activities that cause it, such as cleanings, maintenance calls and tenant turnover, and assigns those costs to each property by how much it actually uses. That reveals each rental's true profit, unlike spreading costs equally.

q: Organizing a database to remove duplicate data and improve its integrity is called
e: Normalization structures a database into related tables so each fact is stored only once. A customer's address lives in one place instead of on every order, which prevents conflicting copies and improves data integrity.

q: An auditor tests whether the first digits of a company's expense amounts follow the expected pattern, in which 1 appears most often. This uses
o: Benford's Law to detect possible fraud
e: Benford's Law predicts that in many naturally occurring data sets, about 30% of numbers start with 1 and fewer than 5% start with 9. Fabricated numbers usually don't follow that pattern, so auditors compare the first-digit distribution of expenses to Benford's to flag possible fraud.

q: A professional who evaluates whether a business or person is likely to repay a loan is a
e: A credit analyst reviews financial statements, credit reports, income and debt to judge whether a borrower is likely to repay, then recommends whether to lend and on what terms. Claims adjusters handle insurance claims, and actuaries calculate risk statistically.

q: Many finance careers, such as stockbroker or insurance agent, require that a person
e: Selling securities requires passing FINRA exams, such as the SIE plus the Series 7 and often the Series 63 or 66, and selling insurance requires a state license exam. Licensing protects consumers by ensuring baseline knowledge and ethics.

q: A relationship in which both people share contacts, advice and referrals so both benefit is described as
e: A reciprocal relationship gives value both ways: each person shares contacts, advice or referrals, and both benefit. Strong professional networks are built on reciprocity, giving as well as asking. One-sided relationships fade quickly.

q: A new financial planner wants to meet other professionals and learn industry trends. A good step is to
o: join and actively participate in a local finance professional association
only email strangers asking for jobs
wait for clients to find her
e: Local finance professional associations, such as a Financial Planning Association chapter, offer networking events, continuing education and industry updates. Participating actively, not just joining, builds relationships, credibility and referrals.

q: An experienced banker who advises a younger colleague on career growth is acting as a
e: A mentor is an experienced professional who shares advice, knowledge and connections to help a less experienced colleague grow. Mentors help with career decisions, skill development and introductions. Competitors, regulators and auditors play different roles.

q: An advisor gives clients a small thank-you when they introduce friends who become clients. This is a
e: A referral system encourages satisfied clients to introduce friends and family, sometimes with a small thank-you, within firm and regulatory rules. Referred clients already trust the advisor through their friend. A pyramid scheme pays people mainly for recruiting, with no real product.

q: Corporate governance helps a company by
o: keeping any one person from having too much unchecked control
e: Good governance creates checks and balances among shareholders, the board and managers, so no one person, not even a powerful CEO, has unchecked control. Independent directors, audit committees and transparent reporting all limit concentrated power.

q: A company with strong corporate governance usually finds it easier to
o: raise money from investors and lenders
e: Investors and lenders trust companies with independent boards, transparent reporting and strong controls because the risk of fraud and mismanagement is lower. That trust makes it easier and cheaper to raise money. Governance doesn't exempt a company from taxes, audits or regulations.

q: After a company's accounting scandal becomes public, what usually happens to investor confidence?
e: An accounting scandal reveals that the numbers investors relied on were wrong and that governance failed. Investors lose confidence, often selling shares, which drives the price down, and lenders may raise borrowing costs. Enron's stock went from about $90 to under $1.

q: Directors who have no business or family ties to the company's managers bring
e: Independent directors have no business, family or financial ties to the company's managers, so they can question management's plans objectively and put shareholders' interests first. NYSE and Nasdaq require a majority of independent directors on listed companies' boards.

q: Board members have a legal duty to act in the best interests of the company and its shareholders. This is a
e: A fiduciary duty is a legal obligation to act in another party's best interest. Directors owe the company and its shareholders a duty of care (informed, careful decisions) and a duty of loyalty (no self-dealing). A warranty is a product promise, and a lien is a claim on property.

q: A main responsibility of a company's board of directors is to
o: set the organization's overall strategic direction and oversee management
write the company's code in software
e: The board sets the organization's overall strategic direction, hires and oversees the CEO and holds management accountable. Managers run daily operations, such as the cash register, customer calls and software development. The board governs; management manages.

q: Which approach best helps employees support a company's governance objectives?
o: Involving employees in achieving the organization's objectives
e: Employees support governance objectives best when they understand them and help achieve them, through training, clear communication and involvement in setting goals. Secrecy, punishing questions or removing the code of conduct would undermine governance.

q: A company links a share of its profits to every employee's pay when governance and performance goals are met. This is
e: Profit-sharing gives employees part of the company's profits when goals are met. It aligns employees' interests with the company's: when the company does well ethically and financially, so do they. Embezzlement is theft, and a stock split changes share count.

q: How does involving employees in governance objectives usually affect them?
o: It increases their sense of purpose and commitment
It makes them ignore company policy
It has no effect on behavior
e: When employees help shape and achieve objectives, they feel ownership. That increases their sense of purpose and commitment to following policies and reaching goals. It adds responsibility rather than removing it.

q: Asking employees for feedback on governance policies helps the company
o: improve its objectives and how they're carried out
e: Front-line employees see how policies work in practice and often spot gaps or problems leaders miss. Their feedback helps the company improve its objectives and how they're carried out. Good governance adapts; it doesn't avoid change or replace the board.

q: An employee notices a coworker falsifying expense reports. Supporting governance objectives, the employee should
o: report it through the company's proper channels, such as an ethics hotline
post about it on social media first
e: Governance depends on employees speaking up. Reporting through proper channels, like an ethics hotline, a supervisor or compliance, lets the company investigate fairly and protects the reporter from retaliation. Ignoring it lets fraud continue, and posting publicly first can harm the investigation.

q: A company sets aside money in its budget to train employees on its new code of conduct. This shows it is
o: allocating resources to achieve governance objectives
e: Governance objectives need resources to succeed. Budgeting money and time to train employees on a new code of conduct shows the company is allocating resources so people understand and follow it. A code no one is trained on rarely changes behavior.

q: When a private company goes public by selling stock on an exchange, its governance structure usually
o: becomes more formal, with independent directors and public reporting
e: Public companies must follow SEC disclosure rules, Sarbanes-Oxley internal-control requirements and stock exchange listing standards, such as a majority of independent directors and an independent audit committee. Their governance becomes more formal and transparent, not less.

q: Which factor most directly affects how complex a company's governance structure needs to be?
e: The more owners a company has, the more it needs formal governance to protect their interests: a board, bylaws, voting rules and regular reporting. A sole proprietor makes every decision alone, while a public company with thousands of shareholders needs extensive structure.

q: A company takes out a large bank loan with covenants that restrict new borrowing and require regular financial reports. This shows that
o: lenders can influence a company's governance
e: Loan covenants are contract terms, such as limits on new debt or required financial reports, that lenders use to protect their money. They shape management's decisions and reporting, showing that creditors are stakeholders who can influence governance, not just shareholders.

q: Government regulations such as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act affect governance structures by
o: requiring controls, independent audit committees and executive certification
e: Sarbanes-Oxley sets minimum governance standards for public companies: internal controls over financial reporting, fully independent audit committees, CEO and CFO certification of reports and protection for whistleblowers. It strengthens boards rather than banning them.

q: Bylaws and governance policies help a company because they
o: outline decision-making processes and protect shareholder rights
e: Bylaws and governance policies spell out who can make which decisions and how: director elections, meeting procedures, voting and approval thresholds. They also protect shareholder rights, such as voting and information. They don't guarantee sales or replace audits.

q: Which group has final authority to approve major decisions such as a merger or hiring a new CEO?
e: Major decisions, such as mergers, hiring or firing the CEO, large investments and dividends, are reserved for the board of directors, which represents shareholders. Some decisions, like a merger, may also need a shareholder vote. Employees, customers and suppliers don't approve them.

q: How do clear governance processes improve management?
o: They clearly define each person's responsibilities and decision rights
They let anyone approve any spending
e: Clear governance processes define who is responsible for what and who can approve which decisions. That reduces confusion, prevents people from overstepping their authority and speeds up good decisions because everyone knows the rules. It increases accountability.

q: Requiring board approval for any purchase over $5 million affects management by
o: adding a check that slows big decisions but improves oversight
e: An approval threshold adds a check on management's biggest decisions. It may slow those decisions slightly, but independent board review reduces the risk of costly mistakes or self-interested deals. Managers still handle everything under the threshold.

q: A board's audit committee reviews financial reports before they're released. This governance process mainly helps
o: ensure the accuracy and reliability of financial reporting
e: The audit committee, made up of independent directors, reviews financial reports before release, oversees internal controls and works with the external auditors. That governance process helps make sure reported numbers are accurate and reliable for investors.

q: Directors who are also company executives (inside directors) usually
o: aren't paid extra for serving on the board
e: Inside directors are company executives, such as the CEO, who also sit on the board. They're compensated through their executive salaries and usually aren't paid extra board fees. They can vote, but they aren't independent, which is why boards also need outside directors.

q: Clear governance helps a company respond faster in a crisis because
o: everyone already knows who has authority to decide
the board must be replaced first
all decisions require a shareholder vote
e: In a crisis, delays are costly. When governance has already defined who has authority to make which decisions, leaders can act immediately instead of debating who's in charge. Clear decision rights speed up response while keeping accountability.

q: When applying for business insurance, why should a company fully disclose its past losses to the underwriter?
o: Honest disclosure is ethical and keeps the policy valid
It always lowers the premium to zero
e: Insurance is based on honest disclosure. Underwriters price the policy on the information provided, and hiding past losses is misrepresentation, which is unethical and can let the insurer deny a claim or cancel the policy. Disclosure keeps the coverage valid when it's needed.

q: An employee reports to regulators that her company is hiding product safety problems. She is a
e: A whistleblower reports wrongdoing, such as hidden safety problems or fraud, to authorities or people who can act. Laws such as Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank protect many whistleblowers from retaliation, and the SEC program can reward them. Underwriters, fiduciaries and brokers have other roles.

q: How are ethics and risk management related?
o: They rely on each other: unethical behavior creates risk
Risk management replaces the need for ethics
e: Ethics and risk management depend on each other. Unethical behavior, like hiding defects, misleading customers or cutting safety corners, creates legal, financial and reputational risk, and a strong ethical culture is one of the best risk controls. Wells Fargo's fake-accounts scandal cost billions.

q: Hiding a product's safety flaws in the fine print of a contract to avoid liability is
o: unethical and increases legal and reputational risk
e: Concealing known safety flaws deceives customers and can cause real harm. It's unethical, can violate consumer protection and product liability laws, and when it comes out, it brings lawsuits, regulatory penalties and lasting reputational damage, increasing risk rather than reducing it.

q: Training employees on workplace ethics expectations helps a company
e: When employees clearly understand what's expected, such as how to handle gifts, conflicts and confidential data, and how to report concerns, many ethical lapses never happen. Training lowers the risk of misconduct and shows regulators the company takes ethics seriously. No program eliminates all risk.

q: Software that watches a network and alerts staff to suspicious access attempts is a(n)
e: An intrusion detection system monitors network traffic and alerts staff to suspicious activity, such as repeated failed logins or unusual data transfers, so possible cyberattacks are caught early. A general ledger records transactions, and word processors and scanners don't monitor security.

q: Which simple practice protects a company from losing financial data in a cyberattack or system failure?
o: Keeping one copy on one laptop
e: Regular, secure backups, ideally kept off-site or separate from the main network, let a company restore its data after a ransomware attack, hardware failure or disaster. Sharing passwords, turning off antivirus and keeping one copy on one laptop all increase the risk of loss.

q: A screen that shows managers real-time charts of key risk measures, such as overdue loans and fraud alerts, is a
e: A digital dashboard displays key measures, such as overdue loans, fraud alerts and cash levels, in real-time charts on one screen. Managers can spot problems at a glance and act quickly. A trial balance lists account balances, and a mission statement states purpose.

q: A bank uses machine learning to flag unusual transactions as they happen. This technology helps
e: Machine learning models learn each customer's normal patterns, such as typical amounts, locations and times, and instantly flag transactions that don't fit for review or blocking. That helps banks detect and stop fraud quickly, often before the customer notices.

q: A company creates its own insurance subsidiary to insure the parent company's risks. This is a
e: A captive insurance company is an insurer owned by the business it insures. The parent pays premiums to its own subsidiary, which can lower costs, cover risks commercial insurers won't and keep underwriting profits within the company. It's a legal risk-financing strategy.

q: Which legal tool lets a business transfer certain risks to another party, such as a supplier agreeing to cover damages from its products?
e: Contracts can transfer risk through indemnification and hold-harmless clauses, for example a supplier agreeing to pay for damages its products cause, or requiring vendors to carry insurance. A press release, mission statement or org chart has no legal effect on risk.

q: Destroying documents to keep them from investigators can lead to charges of
e: Destroying, altering or hiding documents to block an investigation is obstruction of justice. Sarbanes-Oxley added penalties of up to 20 years in prison for destroying records to impede federal investigations, after Arthur Andersen shredded Enron documents.

q: A manufacturer adds clear warning labels and instructions to its products mainly to reduce
e: Inadequate warnings and instructions are a common basis for product liability lawsuits. Clear labels that explain proper use and dangers reduce injuries and give the company a defense if someone misuses the product. It's a risk-control step, not a sales or tax tactic.

q: Following safety and employment laws is part of risk management because it helps a business avoid
e: Breaking safety or employment laws exposes a business to negligence lawsuits, regulatory fines and reputational damage. Compliance reduces that liability exposure, which is why legal compliance is a core part of risk management.

q: A company agrees with its bank to swap its variable-rate loan payments for fixed-rate payments. This controls
e: With a variable-rate loan, rising interest rates would raise the company's payments. An interest rate swap exchanges those variable payments for fixed ones, locking in the cost. It controls interest rate risk, an external economic risk the company can't prevent but can hedge.

q: Changes in inflation and tax rates are examples of risks that are
e: Inflation and tax rates are set by the broader economy and government, so they're external economic risks. A business can't control them, but it can respond with pricing, contracts and planning. Internal risks, like employee error, can be directly controlled.

q: A credit union says no single employee may release a wire over $10,000 without a second sign-off. This is an example of
e: Requiring a second sign-off for large wires is an internal control, a rule the organization creates to prevent errors and fraud. No single person can send a large payment alone, so theft would require collusion. External and market risks come from outside the organization.

q: How does enterprise risk management differ from traditional risk management?
o: ERM looks at the combined impact of all risks across the organization
ERM is used only by small businesses
e: Traditional risk management handles risks separately by department, often focusing on insurable risks. ERM looks at the combined impact of all risks, strategic, operational, financial and compliance, across the whole organization and ties them to strategy, revealing how risks interact.

q: A complete list of the risks an organization faces, used as a starting point for ERM, is a
e: A risk inventory (or risk register) is the complete list of risks an organization faces. ERM starts with identifying risks, then assesses each for likelihood and impact, prioritizes them and assigns owners and responses.

q: Which item reduces retained earnings on a statement of changes in equity?
e: Retained earnings = beginning balance + net income - dividends. Dividends paid to shareholders come out of retained earnings, reducing it. Net income increases it, and issuing stock or owner investments increase contributed capital, a different part of equity.

q: On a statement of owner's equity for a sole proprietorship, new money the owner puts into the business
o: appears only on the income statement
e: For a sole proprietorship, owner's equity = beginning equity + owner investments + net income - owner withdrawals. Money the owner puts into the business increases equity. It isn't revenue, because revenue comes from selling goods or services.

q: Who relies most on the statement of changes in equity to see how their ownership stake changed?
e: The statement of changes in equity shows how the owners' stake changed during the period through net income, dividends, new stock and buybacks. Investors and shareholders rely on it to see whether their ownership value is growing and how profits are being used.

q: The two main parts of shareholders' equity for a corporation are
e: Shareholders' equity has two main parts: capital stock (contributed capital), the money investors paid for shares, and retained earnings, profits kept in the business over time. Payables are liabilities, cash and inventory are assets, and revenue and expenses are income statement items.

q: A company had beginning retained earnings of $80,000, net income of $30,000 and paid $10,000 in dividends. Ending retained earnings are
e: Ending retained earnings = beginning + net income - dividends = $80,000 + $30,000 - $10,000 = $100,000. Net income adds to the profits the company has kept; dividends paid to shareholders take some of them out.

q: A profitable company that chooses not to pay dividends will usually
o: reinvest its retained earnings in the business
e: When a profitable company skips dividends, its profits stay in the business as retained earnings, usually reinvested in growth such as new products, equipment or acquisitions. Many growth companies do this for years. It doesn't mean the company is losing money.

q: Lena deposits $5,000 at 4% interest compounded annually. About how much will she have after 3 years?
e: Compound interest: $5,000 x 1.04 = $5,200 after year 1, x 1.04 = $5,408 after year 2, x 1.04 = $5,624.32 after year 3. Simple interest would give $5,000 + (3 x $200) = $5,600, so compounding adds about $24 from interest on interest.

q: Which change would increase the future value of an investment the most, all else equal?
o: A higher interest rate over more years
e: Future value = PV x (1 + i)^n grows with both the interest rate (i) and the number of periods (n). A higher rate over more years compounds the most. A lower rate, fewer years or withdrawing interest (which stops it compounding) all reduce future value.

q: A company spent $40,000 on market research last year. That cost can't be recovered no matter what it decides now. It is a
e: A sunk cost has already been spent and can't be recovered whatever the company does next. The $40,000 should be ignored when deciding what to do now; only future costs and benefits matter. Variable, differential and opportunity costs are all forward-looking.

q: By choosing to work at his family's shop, Ty gives up a $1,500-a-month job offer. The $1,500 is an example of
e: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative you give up when making a choice. By working at the family shop, Ty gives up the $1,500-a-month job, so that's his opportunity cost. It isn't a sunk cost, because it's about a future choice.

q: The lumber used to build a specific table is a ___ cost of that table.
e: Direct costs can be traced straight to a specific product. The lumber in a table goes directly into that table, so it's a direct (material) cost. Indirect costs, like factory rent, are shared across products and must be allocated.

q: A factory's building insurance is shared by all the products made there. For each product, it's a(n)
e: Building insurance benefits everything made in the factory and can't be traced to one product, so it's an indirect cost (overhead). It's assigned to products through allocation, for example by machine hours or square footage.

q: When choosing between two suppliers, a manager compares only the costs that differ between them. These are
e: Differential (incremental) costs are the costs that differ between alternatives. Costs that are the same either way don't affect the choice, and sunk costs are already spent. Focusing on differences makes the comparison clear and accurate.

q: A bakery should keep increasing production as long as each additional batch brings
o: marginal revenue equal to or greater than its marginal cost
e: Profit rises as long as each additional batch brings in at least as much revenue as it costs to make (marginal revenue at least equal to marginal cost). When marginal cost exceeds marginal revenue, extra batches start reducing profit, so that's where production should stop.

q: Looking at the extra cost and extra revenue of producing one more unit is called
e: Marginal analysis focuses on the change, the additional (marginal) revenue and cost of producing one more unit or making one more decision. It's used for pricing, production levels and special orders. Horizontal analysis compares statements over time, and SWOT assesses strategy.

q: Besides the numbers, marginal analysis of a decision should also consider
o: qualitative factors, such as customer goodwill and employee morale
e: Some effects of a decision can't be measured precisely in dollars, like customer goodwill, employee morale, brand reputation or quality. Good marginal analysis weighs these qualitative factors alongside the numbers, since a profitable decision that angers loyal customers may not be wise.

q: A factory has idle capacity. A customer offers to buy 1,000 units at $9 each. Each unit costs $6 in variable costs, and fixed costs won't change. Accepting the order would
e: With idle capacity, fixed costs don't change, so only marginal (variable) costs matter. Each unit earns $9 and costs $6, a $3 contribution, so 1,000 units x $3 = $3,000 more profit. The order makes sense as long as it doesn't hurt regular full-price sales.

q: A manager uses marginal analysis to decide whether to
e: Marginal analysis fits incremental decisions about adding or cutting an activity, such as adding a second shift, producing more units or extending hours. The manager compares the extra revenue with the extra cost. Naming a company or writing a mission statement isn't a marginal decision.

q: The cost of producing one additional unit is the
e: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from producing one more unit, usually the variable cost of that unit, such as materials and labor. Average fixed cost is fixed cost per unit, and sunk costs are already spent.

q: Because of diminishing returns, as a business keeps adding workers to the same equipment, the marginal output of each new worker eventually
e: The law of diminishing returns says that adding more of one input, like workers, to a fixed amount of another, like equipment, eventually produces smaller and smaller increases in output. Workers start sharing machines and getting in each other's way, so each new worker adds less.

q: How is managerial accounting different from financial accounting?
o: It takes a future-focused approach for internal decisions
It reports only to the IRS
It is published for outside investors
e: Managerial accounting is future-focused and prepared for internal managers to plan, control and decide, with no required format. Financial accounting reports past results to outsiders, such as investors, lenders and the IRS, following GAAP. Managerial reports aren't published publicly.

q: A marketing manager compares the relevant costs of a TV campaign and a social media campaign before choosing. This is an application of
e: Comparing the relevant costs of two options before choosing is a classic managerial accounting application: it supports an internal decision. External auditing checks financial statements for outsiders, and tax and payroll accounting have their own narrow purposes.

q: Managerial accounting reports are prepared mainly for
e: Managerial accounting reports, such as budgets, cost analyses and product profitability, are prepared for managers inside the company to plan, control and decide. Regulators, the public and competitors see financial accounting reports, not internal managerial ones.

q: Classifying costs by whether a department manager can influence them helps evaluate managers fairly. This is classification by
e: Classifying costs by controllability separates costs a manager can influence, like supplies and overtime, from those they can't, like the building's rent. Judging managers only on controllable costs is fair and motivates them to manage what they can actually change.

q: Managerial accountants accumulate data on the costs and profits of each product line so managers can
o: decide which products to expand or drop
e: By tracking the costs and profits of each product line, managerial accountants show which products earn the most and which lose money. Managers use that to decide which products to expand, reprice or drop. Tax returns and annual reports are financial accounting tasks.

q: Managerial accounting both ___ financial data and ___ it for decision-makers.
e: Managerial accountants do both: they record (gather and accumulate) financial and operating data, such as costs by product or department, and they interpret it, explaining what it means so managers can plan and decide. Interpretation is what makes it useful for decisions.

q: A store's storage costs were budgeted at $5,000 but actually came to $6,200. This difference is a(n)
e: Variance = actual - budget = $6,200 - $5,000 = $1,200. When actual costs exceed budget, the variance is unfavorable because it reduces profit. The manager should find out why storage cost more, such as more inventory or higher rent, and adjust.

q: A company paid more per pound for raw materials than its standard cost. Which variance does this create?
e: A purchase (materials) price variance occurs when the actual price paid differs from the standard price: (actual price - standard price) x quantity purchased. Paying more per pound creates an unfavorable price variance. Labor efficiency variances concern hours worked, not material prices.

q: Variance analysis compares ___ results with ___ results.
e: Variance analysis compares planned (budgeted or standard) results with actual results: variance = actual - planned. The size and direction of each difference show where performance departed from the plan. It isn't a comparison with competitors or between gross and net figures.

q: After finding a large labor variance on a project, a manager should
o: investigate the cause and make appropriate adjustments
e: Variance analysis is only useful if it leads to action. The manager should investigate why labor ran over, such as underestimated tasks, scope creep, inexperienced staff or equipment problems, then adjust the plan or future estimates. Ignoring it or firing everyone doesn't fix the cause.

q: A marketing budget shows a favorable variance because planned email campaigns were never sent. This shows that
o: a favorable variance can still signal a problem
e: Spending under budget looks favorable, but here it happened because planned email campaigns were never sent, so the work that drives sales wasn't done. Future sales may suffer. Every variance, favorable or not, should be investigated for its cause.

q: Tracking variances regularly helps managers
e: Budgetary control means using the budget as a standard and regularly comparing actual results against it, so problems are caught and corrected early instead of at year-end. Variance tracking is the main tool. It doesn't replace planning, raise prices or remove fixed costs.

q: Cost accounting budgets help managers mainly by serving as a
o: financial control tool to compare and evaluate performance
e: Cost budgets set the expected cost of production, and comparing actual costs with them shows whether departments controlled spending. That makes them a financial control tool for evaluating performance. They don't replace financial statements, tax returns or marketing plans.

q: In the management functions, using a cost budget to tell departments how much they can spend is part of
e: Directing is guiding people's work toward goals. A cost budget directs activity by telling each department how much it can spend and on what, so their effort and resources line up with the plan. Recruiting is a staffing task, and advertising is marketing.

q: A production budget that shows total costs of making goods, including materials, labor and overhead, helps management
o: consider the business's total cost of production
e: A production cost budget brings together direct materials, direct labor and manufacturing overhead, so management sees the total cost of producing goods. That's essential for pricing, planning cash needs and checking profitability. It doesn't set competitors' prices or calculate dividends.

q: A cost that rises and falls in direct proportion to production, such as packaging, is a ___ cost in a cost budget.
e: Variable costs change in direct proportion to production volume: make twice as many units and packaging costs roughly double. Fixed costs, like rent and salaries, stay the same in the short run regardless of volume. Cost budgets separate the two to plan accurately.

q: Comparing actual production costs to the cost budget helps a company
e: Comparing actual production costs with the cost budget reveals variances, places where spending was higher or lower than planned. Investigating them uncovers waste, price changes or process problems, so the company can improve efficiency.

q: Cost budgets help define roles because they
o: assign spending responsibility to specific managers
e: Each line of a cost budget is assigned to a specific manager who's responsible for staying within it. That clarifies who is accountable for which costs and gives each manager authority over their area. It increases accountability rather than removing it.

q: Using a cost budget to judge how well a production manager controlled costs is an example of using budgets to
e: A cost budget sets a benchmark for what costs should be. Comparing a manager's actual costs with it shows how well they controlled spending, so budgets are used to evaluate performance. Fair evaluation also considers whether the costs were within the manager's control.

q: Assigning a share of the building's electricity bill to each department based on square footage is an example of
e: Cost allocation divides a shared, indirect cost, like a building's electricity, among departments using an allocation base that reflects use, here square footage. A department with 25% of the space gets 25% of the bill. It doesn't change the total cost, only how it's distributed.

q: Which cost is most likely to be allocated among departments rather than traced directly?
o: A sales commission on one sale
Hourly wages of one product's assembler
e: Electricity for the whole building serves every department, and there's usually no meter per department, so it can't be traced directly and must be allocated. Raw materials for one product, a commission on one sale and wages of one product's assembler are direct costs.

q: Costs are allocated when
o: a cost isn't controlled by or traceable to a single department
a cost belongs to one product only
the cost has already been refunded
e: Allocation is needed when a cost is shared and can't be traced to or controlled by a single department or product, such as rent, utilities, IT or a CEO's salary. Costs that belong entirely to one product are simply assigned directly.

q: A bank divides its call center costs among branches based on how many customers each branch serves. The allocation base is
e: The allocation base is the measure used to divide a shared cost. Here it's the number of customers each branch serves, a sensible choice because more customers likely means more calls. A good base reflects what actually drives the cost.

q: Allocation moves ___ costs to departments or products so they can be added to ___ costs for a full cost picture.
e: Allocation assigns indirect (shared) costs to departments or products, where they're added to the direct costs already traced there. Direct costs plus allocated indirect costs give the full cost, which managers need for pricing and profitability decisions.

q: Why does cost allocation matter for pricing?
o: Without it, a product's price might not cover its full share of overhead
It always lowers prices to zero
e: If overhead isn't allocated, a product's cost looks lower than it really is, and its price might cover materials and labor but not its share of rent, utilities and administration. Over time that loses money. Allocation helps set prices that cover all costs and earn a profit.

q: As the economy moves from recession into recovery, investors tend to
o: buy stocks, expecting profits to rise
e: Investors price stocks on expected future earnings. As the economy moves from recession toward recovery, they anticipate rising sales and profits, so they tend to buy stocks, often before the recovery shows up in jobs data. That's why markets often bottom before the economy does.

q: Which institution lends to developing countries for projects like roads and schools to reduce poverty?
e: The World Bank Group provides loans, grants and expertise to governments of developing countries for projects like roads, schools, health care and clean water, with the goal of reducing poverty. The FDIC insures U.S. deposits, and credit unions and brokerages serve individual customers.

q: Stocks of small companies that aren't listed on a major exchange often trade
e: Securities not listed on a major exchange like the NYSE or Nasdaq trade over the counter (OTC), directly between dealers through networks such as the OTC Markets Group. OTC stocks are often smaller, less liquid and riskier, with lighter disclosure requirements.

q: Which finance career focuses on evaluating risks and deciding whether to issue an insurance policy and at what price?
e: An insurance underwriter evaluates applicants' risk, such as health, driving record or property condition, and decides whether to issue a policy and at what premium. Investment bank underwriters do something similar for new securities. Tellers, planners and collectors have different roles.

q: A client is confused by a fund's prospectus. A responsible advisor should
o: explain the benefits and drawbacks in simple terms
tell the client not to worry about it
e: Part of a finance professional's responsibility is making sure clients understand what they're buying. A responsible advisor explains both the benefits and the drawbacks, including risks and fees, in plain language so the client can make an informed decision. Explaining only the benefits is misleading.

q: An analyst needs a list of only clients in Springfield with balances over $250,000. The fastest database tool is
e: A database query with filters, such as city = Springfield AND balance > $250,000, instantly returns exactly the matching records. Retyping records is slow and error-prone, a pie chart displays data rather than selecting it, and a word-processing template isn't a database tool.

q: Which ratio type shows how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate sales?
e: Asset utilization (turnover) ratios, such as total asset turnover = sales / total assets, show how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate sales. Higher turnover means more sales per dollar of assets. Liquidity ratios measure ability to pay short-term bills.

q: A bank compares the debt-to-income ratios of loan applicants with its credit standards. If an applicant's DTI is 52% and the limit is 43%, the bank will most likely
e: Credit standards set the maximum risk a lender will accept. A 52% DTI means more than half the applicant's income already goes to debt, well above the bank's 43% limit, so the bank will likely decline the loan or restructure it, for example as a smaller amount or with a cosigner.

q: Financial globalization has been driven partly by
o: internet-based financial transactions and fewer capital controls
e: Financial globalization grew as the internet made cross-border transactions instant and cheap, and as countries reduced capital controls and deregulated markets. Money can now move around the world in seconds. Banning trade, fixing exchange rates or closing exchanges would do the opposite.

q: Under ERM, organizations are encouraged to view some risks as
o: always negative and to be avoided
e: Enterprise risk management treats risk as two-sided: some risks, such as entering a new market or launching a product, can create value if managed well. ERM ties risk to strategy instead of seeing it only as something to avoid or insure.

q: Installing security cameras in a bank branch is a form of
o: risk control to reduce theft losses
e: Security cameras deter theft and help catch thieves, lowering both the likelihood and the cost of losses. That's risk control (reduction). Risk transfer would be buying insurance, and risk retention would be accepting losses without action.

q: Why does ethical financial-information management make a company more attractive to investors?
o: Accurate, honest data builds trust, which makes it easier to raise money
It guarantees a higher stock price
e: Investors and lenders need to trust a company's numbers before committing money. Accurate, honest financial information builds that trust and lowers perceived risk, making it easier and cheaper to raise money. Ethics can't guarantee a higher stock price or remove business risk.

q: An estate passing directly to a surviving spouse is generally
o: not subject to federal estate tax because of the unlimited marital deduction
e: The unlimited marital deduction lets a person leave any amount to a U.S.-citizen spouse free of federal estate tax. Taxes may apply later when the surviving spouse's estate passes to others, above the exemption ($15 million per person in 2026).

q: Who benefits from good corporate governance?
o: All stakeholders: shareholders, employees, customers and communities
e: Good governance balances the interests of all stakeholders: shareholders get honest management and better returns, employees get fair treatment and stable jobs, customers get trustworthy products and communities get responsible corporate citizens. It's not designed to benefit just the CEO.

q: An internal audit function in a well-governed company mainly
o: tests internal controls and checks that policies are followed
e: Internal auditors independently test whether internal controls work and whether policies and laws are followed, then report findings to management and the board's audit committee. That gives leaders assurance that risks are managed. Pricing, advertising and hiring belong to other functions.

q: A major risk that comes with storing financial data online is
e: Data stored online can be reached from anywhere, which also makes it a target for hackers. A cybersecurity breach can expose sensitive financial and customer data, leading to losses, fines and lost trust. Faster reporting, lower printing costs and easier collaboration are benefits, not risks.

q: A business owner tracks actual spending against the budget every month using software. This step of budgeting is
e: Tracking (monitoring) compares actual spending with the budget regularly, monthly here, so overspending is caught early and the plan can be adjusted. A budget that isn't tracked is just a guess. Budgeting software makes this comparison quick.

q: Getting a paycheck deposited a week earlier and investing it right away helps because
o: the money can start earning interest sooner
interest rates are higher on Mondays
e: Time is a key driver of the time value of money: the sooner money is invested, the longer it earns interest and compounds. Even small head starts add up over many years. Interest rates don't change by day of the week, and investing doesn't avoid taxes.

q: Combining the financial statements of a parent company and its subsidiaries into one set of statements is called
o: a statement of changes in equity only
e: Consolidated financial statements combine the assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses of a parent company and its subsidiaries into one set, as if they were a single company. Investors see the whole group's financial picture. Transactions between the companies are eliminated.

q: Software that reads new regulations, flags which ones apply to a bank and assigns tasks to update its policies is used for
e: Regulatory change management tools track new and updated rules, identify which apply to the firm, and assign tasks to update policies, procedures and training. Regulations change constantly, so technology helps firms stay compliant without missing anything.

q: In an agency relationship, the agent must
o: act in the best interest of the principal
act in the agent's own best interest
e: In an agency relationship, the agent acts on behalf of the principal, such as an employee for an employer or a broker for a client, and owes fiduciary duties: loyalty, obedience to lawful instructions, reasonable care and accounting for money. The agent must put the principal's interests first.

q: Laws that limit pollution and protect natural resources are examples of
e: Environmental law protects air, water, land and wildlife from harmful business and human activity, through laws like the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act enforced by the EPA. Businesses must comply or face fines and cleanup costs. Contract law governs agreements.

q: Rules that limit how many fish a company can catch each season to protect future supplies are a form of
e: Conservation laws manage natural resources so they aren't used up, for example fishing quotas, hunting seasons and limits on logging. They protect future supplies for businesses and communities. Antitrust law addresses competition, and labor law addresses employment.

q: A disease kills many orange trees, so fewer oranges reach the market. If demand stays the same, the price of oranges will most likely
e: When supply falls and demand stays the same, there are fewer oranges for the same number of buyers. Prices rise until enough buyers drop out that the smaller supply is enough. Rising prices ration scarce goods and signal growers to produce more.

q: A risk that could produce either a gain or a loss, such as launching a new product, is a
e: Speculative risk can result in a gain, a loss or no change, such as launching a new product, investing or expanding. Pure risk can only result in a loss or no loss, such as a fire or theft, which is why pure risks are generally insurable and speculative risks are not.

q: A snowstorm closes a store for three days. This is an example of a
e: Natural risks come from nature: storms, floods, earthquakes and fires caused by lightning. A snowstorm closing a store is a natural risk. Human risks come from people (theft, errors), and market risks from economic conditions.

q: Assigning each worker one repeated task on an assembly line is an example of
e: Division of labor (specialization) breaks work into tasks and assigns each worker one task, which they repeat and become fast and skilled at. It usually raises productivity. Job enrichment adds variety and responsibility, and job rotation moves workers between tasks.

q: A drawback of very narrow job specialization is that workers may
o: become bored and their skills may become obsolete
e: Doing the same small task over and over can become boring, lowering morale and increasing turnover. Very narrow skills may also become obsolete if technology automates that task. Companies counter this with job rotation and enrichment.

q: When doing business with clients from another culture, a finance professional should
o: learn their customs and strive to communicate clearly
assume their customs match their own
e: Learning a client's customs, such as greetings, communication style, attitudes toward time and decision-making, and communicating clearly shows respect and prevents misunderstandings. Assuming everyone shares your customs, speaking fast or using slang can confuse or offend.

q: A gesture that's friendly in one country can be insulting in another. This shows that global business is affected by
e: Cultural and social environments, including values, customs, language and nonverbal communication, differ across countries. A thumbs-up or an 'OK' sign means different things in different places, so international business requires cultural awareness.

q: A tax that takes a larger percentage of income from people with higher incomes is
e: A progressive tax takes a larger percentage of income as income rises; the federal income tax, with rates from 10% to 37%, is progressive. A regressive tax takes a larger share from lower-income people (sales taxes tend to be), and a proportional tax uses one rate for everyone.

q: Organizing a bank's departments around retail customers, business customers and wealthy clients is organizing by
e: Organizing by customer type groups work around the kinds of customers served, such as retail, business and wealthy clients, so each department can specialize in their needs. Businesses can also organize by function, product or geography.

q: Whatever its structure, the organizational design of a for-profit business ultimately aims to help it
o: earn a profit by meeting customer needs efficiently
e: A for-profit business's structure exists to help it reach its goals, ultimately earning a profit by meeting customer needs efficiently. Good design clarifies roles, speeds decisions and puts resources where they create the most value. More paperwork isn't the goal.

q: A main benefit of regular staff communication between managers and employees is that it
o: creates opportunities for feedback and suggestions
e: Regular two-way communication gives employees chances to give feedback and suggest improvements, and gives managers early warning of problems. It improves morale and decisions. It doesn't eliminate meetings, guarantee promotions or replace training.

q: An informational message to employees about a new expense policy should mainly
o: explain the policy clearly and completely
persuade them to buy a product
e: An informational message's purpose is to make sure readers understand facts they need, here the new policy: what changed, who it applies to, when it starts and how to follow it. It should be clear and complete. Persuading, entertaining or criticizing would be different purposes.

q: Which behavior helps a group discussion?
o: Asking questions to clarify others' comments
Checking your phone while others talk
e: Asking questions to clarify others' comments shows you're listening, prevents misunderstandings and keeps the discussion productive. Blurting out statements, interrupting to change the subject and checking your phone all disrupt the group.

q: In a group discussion, a member who proposes a direction for the group to follow is
e: Proposing a direction or plan for the group is a positive group role, sometimes called initiating, that sets the group's course and moves the discussion forward. Blocking, withdrawing and dominating are negative roles that hurt group progress.

q: Before using an article's data in a report, you should first
o: check the author's credentials and the source's credibility
make sure it's the longest article
e: Before relying on information, check its credibility: who the author is and what qualifies them, who published it, whether it cites sources and how current it is. Using unreliable data can lead to wrong conclusions. Length, pictures or being online don't make a source valid.

q: Which is a sign that written material is likely reliable?
o: The author lists relevant professional qualifications and cites sources
It's an anonymous social media post
e: Reliable material usually comes from an author with relevant professional qualifications, published by a reputable source, with cited evidence you can check. Anonymous posts, unattributed content and emotional formatting like many exclamation points are warning signs.

q: When a colleague disagrees with your proposal in a meeting, the best way to defend it objectively is to
o: acknowledge their concerns and present facts that support your view
e: Defending an idea objectively means acknowledging the other person's concerns respectfully and responding with facts and reasoning that support your view.
