That keeps the discussion professional and persuasive. Raising your voice, attacking the person or refusing to discuss it undermines your credibility.

q: How should you prepare for a staff meeting?
o: Read important documents and do research ahead of time
Arrive late to avoid small talk
Plan to decide everything in the meeting
e: Preparing, by reading the agenda and documents and doing any research ahead of time, lets you contribute useful ideas and make decisions efficiently. It respects everyone's time. Arriving late or bringing unrelated work signals you don't value the meeting.

q: During a staff meeting, it's appropriate to ask a question when
o: you want to change the subject to your weekend
e: Asking a question when you need a point clarified keeps everyone on the same page and prevents mistakes later. Changing the subject, asking about things covered in the agenda you didn't read or interrupting someone mid-sentence is disruptive.

q: To show a client what percentage of her portfolio is in stocks, bonds and cash right now, the best graphic aid is a
e: A pie chart shows how a whole divides into parts at one point in time, so it's ideal for a portfolio's mix, such as 60% stocks, 30% bonds and 10% cash. Line graphs show trends over time, bar charts compare amounts across categories and organizational charts show reporting structure. Use percentages that add to 100%.

q: An executive summary is written mainly for
o: busy readers who don't have time to read the full report
e: Executives and other busy decision makers often don't have time to read a full report. The executive summary gives them the key findings and recommendations up front, in a page or so, and must make sense on its own. Supporting detail stays in the body and appendices.

q: A drawback of purely verbal instructions is that they
e: Spoken instructions leave no record, so listeners may forget details or remember them differently. That's why important verbal instructions, like deadlines, numbers and procedures, should be followed up in writing. Verbal messages can include details; they're just harder to retain.

q: Effective verbal communication relies on
o: using as much jargon as possible
e: Effective speakers use precise, clear words, speak at a moderate pace and match their language to the audience, so listeners understand and remember the message. Heavy jargon confuses non-experts, speaking too fast loses listeners and avoiding eye contact reduces trust.

q: Effective communication is best described as
o: a two-way process of sharing and understanding
one person talking while others listen
sending as many emails as possible
e: Communication is a two-way process: a sender shares a message, the receiver interprets it and responds with feedback. It succeeds only when the receiver understands the intended meaning. One-way talking, flooding inboxes or avoiding feedback doesn't ensure understanding.

q: In a job interview, which nonverbal behavior communicates confidence and interest?
e: Appropriate eye contact signals confidence, honesty and interest in the conversation. Looking at the floor suggests nervousness or disinterest, crossed arms look defensive and checking the time suggests you want to leave.

q: When creating presentation slides for a client meeting, you should
o: use bullet points organized by topic and readable fonts
fill each slide with full paragraphs
e: Effective slides are simple and organized: short bullet points grouped by topic, clear headings and readable fonts, so the audience can follow while listening to you. Full paragraphs make people read instead of listen, and decorative fonts are hard to read.

q: Repeating a company's name and page number at the bottom of every slide is done with a
e: A footer is text, like a company name, slide or page number or date, that automatically appears at the bottom of every slide or page. A header does the same at the top. Pivot tables summarize data, and a macro virus is malware.

q: A client complains about a fee. The employee resolving it should offer
o: solutions available within the business's policies
whatever the customer demands, regardless of policy
no response until the customer calms down on their own
e: Resolving complaints within company policy is fair to every customer and protects the business. The employee should listen, explain and offer the solutions policy allows, such as a one-time courtesy waiver or a way to avoid the fee. Promising whatever is demanded, or something they can't deliver, causes bigger problems.

q: Software that automates sales tasks such as tracking leads, scheduling follow-ups and forecasting sales is
e: Sales force automation is a CRM feature that automates sales tasks, such as tracking leads, scheduling follow-ups, logging contacts and forecasting sales, so salespeople spend more time with customers and less on paperwork. Payroll and firewalls serve other purposes.

q: Mobile CRM apps on smartphones help financial advisors
o: access client information and update records while away from the office
e: Mobile CRM apps let advisors look up client information and update records right after a meeting, wherever they are. Client data stays current and service stays responsive. They don't replace client conversations or remove the need for data security.

q: A shopper buys a more expensive watch than usual because it's a gift. This purchase was influenced by
e: Situational influences, such as the purpose of the purchase, time pressure and the setting, affect buying behavior. Buying a gift often leads people to spend more than they would on themselves. The store's accounting method and the interest rate don't drive this choice.

q: An employee checks in with customers to see whether they need additional products. This action helps the company
o: achieve its sales goals and strengthen relationships
e: Proactively checking in shows customers you care about their needs, which builds relationships and often uncovers needs the company can meet. That helps the company reach its sales and satisfaction goals. It creates value rather than adding cost without benefit.

q: The main purpose of feedback from a supervisor is to help you
o: improve your ability to do the job
e: Feedback tells you what you're doing well and what to improve, so you can grow and do your job better. Constructive feedback is about improvement, not embarrassment or comparison with others.

q: When receiving critical feedback, the best first response is to
o: listen calmly and ask questions to understand
e: Listening calmly and asking questions to understand the feedback shows maturity and openness, and makes sure you know exactly what to improve. Arguing, getting angry or ignoring it blocks growth and damages your relationship with your supervisor.

q: A new employee assumes all older clients dislike technology. This is an example of
e: A stereotype is an oversimplified belief that everyone in a group shares the same traits. Many older clients use technology comfortably. Professionals should treat each client as an individual, ask about preferences and set aside assumptions.

q: An employee who refuses to try any new procedure and complains about every change is showing
e: A positive attitude includes adaptability, being open to change and willing to learn. Refusing every new procedure and constantly complaining shows a negative, inflexible attitude that hurts teamwork and career growth.

q: Avoiding situations that trigger impulsive spending, such as deleting shopping apps, is a self-control strategy called
e: Stimulus control means changing your environment to remove triggers for unwanted behavior, such as deleting shopping apps, unsubscribing from sale emails or not saving card numbers online. It makes self-control easier because you face fewer temptations.

q: Which is a common effect of high stress in the workplace?
o: Low morale and more interpersonal conflict
e: Unmanaged workplace stress lowers morale, increases conflict between coworkers and leads to more mistakes, absences and turnover. It can also hurt sleep and health. That's why stress management matters for individuals and organizations.

q: A coworker asks you about a client's account balance for no business reason. You should
o: share it since they work at the company
post it in the break room
e: Client information should be shared only with people who need it for legitimate business purposes. A coworker's curiosity isn't a business reason, so you should keep the information confidential. Sharing it violates the client's privacy and possibly privacy laws.

q: A company asks employees to sign a nondisclosure agreement mainly to
e: A nondisclosure agreement (NDA) is a contract in which employees agree not to share the company's confidential or proprietary information, such as trade secrets, client lists and financial data. It protects the company's competitive advantage and clients.

q: A personal vision is most useful when it
o: accurately reflects what you want from life
focuses only on what others expect
e: A personal vision is a picture of who you want to be and what you want from life. It's most useful when it truly reflects your own values and goals, not a friend's or others' expectations, so it can guide your decisions consistently.

q: Having a personal vision helps you
o: have a clear picture of your goals in life
e: A personal vision gives you a clear picture of your goals in life, which helps you set specific goals, make choices about school, career and money and stay motivated. It guides planning; it doesn't replace it or remove risk.

q: Which habit makes it hardest to manage commitments on time?
e: Procrastination, putting tasks off until later, leaves too little time to finish, causing rushed work and missed deadlines. Using a calendar, estimating task time and prioritizing all help you meet commitments.

q: Before agreeing to a new assignment, a reliable employee should
o: estimate how long it will take and check current workload
wait until the deadline to start
ask a coworker to do it
e: Reliable people estimate how long a new task will take and check their current workload before committing. That prevents overcommitting and missed deadlines. Saying yes to everything, waiting until the deadline or passing work to coworkers makes you unreliable.

q: A manager who encourages employees to use and develop their talents is
e: Inspiring others means motivating people to grow, use their talents and work toward goals they care about. Encouraging employees to develop their abilities builds engagement and loyalty. Micromanaging controls every detail, which discourages growth.

q: Inspired employees are typically
o: driven to take action toward shared goals
e: Inspired employees feel connected to a shared purpose, so they're motivated to take initiative and act toward common goals, often going beyond what's required. They tend to be more productive and open to change.

q: Brainstorming in a team meeting is a technique for
o: generating many creative ideas without judging them at first
e: Brainstorming generates as many ideas as possible in a short time, without judging them at first. Withholding criticism encourages creative, unusual ideas, which can be combined and evaluated later. Choosing immediately or criticizing every idea shuts creativity down.

q: Taking an interest inventory helps a student
o: see the kinds of work they might enjoy
e: An interest inventory is a questionnaire that matches your interests to types of work and careers you might enjoy. It helps you explore options and plan education. It can't guarantee a job, set a salary or replace classes.

q: Working mainly for a high salary rather than enjoyment of the work is an example of
e: Extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards like pay, bonuses, grades or praise. Intrinsic motivation comes from enjoying the work itself or finding it meaningful. Most people have both, but intrinsic motivation tends to sustain effort longer.

q: On a job application, a question that doesn't apply to you should be answered with
e: Writing 'does not apply' or 'N/A' shows the employer you read and considered every question. A blank space can look like you skipped or overlooked it, and made-up answers are dishonest.

q: Information on a job application should be
o: accurate and consistent with your résumé
e: A job application should be accurate, complete and consistent with your résumé. Employers compare the two, and differences in dates, titles or details raise doubts about honesty. Applications should be neat and specific, not vague.

q: Researching a company before an interview helps you
o: ask good questions and show genuine interest
e: Researching the company's products, values, recent news and culture lets you ask thoughtful questions, connect your skills to its needs and show genuine interest. Interviewers notice preparation. It doesn't replace answering questions or preparing your own answers.

q: Which resource helps a finance professional stay current on industry trends?
e: Trade publications and professional journals cover industry news, regulatory changes, new products and best practices, which helps finance professionals stay current. Examples include American Banker and the Journal of Financial Planning.

q: Professional and trade associations often work to
o: offer training and influence legislation affecting their industry
e: Professional and trade associations offer training, certifications, conferences and networking, and they advocate for their industry by working to influence legislation and regulation. They don't set members' prices (that could be illegal price-fixing) or replace regulators.

q: Assigning a new hire an experienced 'buddy' during the first weeks helps
o: the new employee learn the ropes faster
e: A buddy or mentor helps a new employee learn unwritten rules, answers everyday questions and introduces them to coworkers, so they adjust and become productive faster. It supports, but doesn't replace, formal orientation and training.

q: A written description of the skills, education and experience a job requires is a
e: A job specification lists the qualifications, including skills, education, experience and certifications, a person needs for a job. A job description lists the job's duties and responsibilities. Employers use both to recruit and screen candidates.

q: Which activity best shows entrepreneurship?
o: Developing and selling a new product to meet an unmet need
Working the same job for a large company
e: Entrepreneurship means identifying an unmet need and taking the risk to create a business that meets it, such as developing and selling a new product. Working for a large company is employment, buying stock is investing and paying bills is routine financial management.

q: Why do ethical practices benefit an entrepreneur's business?
o: Many customers prefer to support companies that act ethically
Ethics always lowers costs to zero
Ethics removes the need for a business plan
e: Small businesses depend on reputation and trust. Many customers prefer to buy from companies that treat people fairly and act ethically, and word of mouth spreads quickly. Ethical practices also attract and keep good employees. Ethics doesn't make costs zero or replace planning.

q: A couple planning to combine their finances should first
o: share and agree on their financial goals
open as many credit cards as possible
hide their debts from each other
e: Before combining finances, a couple should openly share and agree on their goals, such as saving for a home, paying off debt or retirement, plus their debts and spending habits. Shared goals prevent conflict and guide joint decisions. Hiding debts or opening many cards causes problems.

q: When should you record a debit card purchase or a check in your account register?
o: As soon as you make it
At the end of the year
e: Record every debit purchase or check as soon as you make it, so your register always shows how much you actually have available. Waiting can lead to overdrafts because pending transactions may not appear in the bank's balance yet.

q: When balancing an account, monthly service fees shown on the bank statement should be
e: Bank service fees reduce your balance, so when you balance your account you subtract them from your register, along with any other bank charges, and add any interest earned. Then your register should match the adjusted bank statement.

q: An accountant who reports numbers accurately even when it displeases her manager is demonstrating
e: Objectivity means reporting facts without bias, and integrity means being honest even under pressure. Reporting accurate numbers that displease a manager demonstrates both, which are core values in the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct.

q: Small unethical shortcuts that slowly grow into major misconduct are an example of
e: Incrementalism, the slippery slope, is when small ethical compromises gradually become normal and lead to bigger ones. A small 'temporary' adjustment can grow into fraud, as at WorldCom. Recognizing the first small step is key to stopping it.

q: An investor who believes they can't make a mistake and ignores risk warnings shows the bias called
e: Overconfidence bias leads people to overestimate their knowledge or ability and underestimate risk, which causes excessive trading, poor diversification and ignored warnings. Loss aversion is feeling losses more strongly than gains, a different bias.

q: Recording customers' purchasing habits and payment history in a database helps a business
o: serve customers better and manage credit
e: Customer records showing purchases and payment history help a business understand what customers want, personalize service and marketing, and make sound credit decisions about who can buy on credit and how much. Accurate records reduce errors.

q: Which document is usually kept in a customer's file as a record of what was sold and how much is owed?
e: An invoice records what was sold, the quantity, price, total owed and payment terms. Businesses keep invoices in customer files to track sales and amounts due. Mission statements, org charts and press releases aren't customer records.

q: Studying changes in the economy, laws, technology, society and competitors that might affect a business is called
e: Environmental scanning is the ongoing study of external factors, such as economic, political and legal, social, technological and competitive changes, that could create opportunities or threats for a business. Bookkeeping, payroll and inventory counts are internal tasks.

q: Why must environmental scanning be done continuously?
o: The external environment is dynamic and changes constantly
It's required only once by law
e: The external environment is dynamic: interest rates move, laws change, competitors launch products and customer tastes shift. Information gathered once quickly goes out of date, so businesses must scan continuously to spot new opportunities and threats.

q: A bank researching how popular a competitor's new mobile app is with customers is scanning the
e: Researching a competitor's new app is scanning the competitive environment, part of the external environment. Knowing what rivals offer and how customers respond helps the bank decide whether to improve its own app or respond in other ways.

q: Information systems help managers mainly by
o: supporting the decision-making process with timely information
e: Information systems collect, store, process and deliver data so managers have timely, accurate information for decisions. They support managers rather than replacing them.

q: A system that stores every customer interaction and purchase so staff can personalize service is a
e: A customer relationship management (CRM) system is an information system that stores customer data, interactions and purchase history so staff can personalize service and spot needs. Payroll systems manage pay, firewalls protect networks and general ledgers record transactions.

q: A set of loan amounts is $5,000, $7,000, $7,000, $9,000 and $12,000. What is the median?
e: The median is the middle value of an ordered list. With five values ($5,000, $7,000, $7,000, $9,000, $12,000), the third is $7,000. The mean (average) is $40,000 / 5 = $8,000, a common trap answer. The mode, the most frequent value, is also $7,000.

q: Analysts study the spread of investment returns, such as the standard deviation, mainly to
e: Standard deviation measures how widely returns spread around the average. A larger spread means returns swing more, so the investment is more volatile and riskier. Investors use it to compare risk between investments.

q: Information management helps a business
o: reduce risk and comply with government regulations
e: Good information management keeps records organized, secure, accurate and retrievable. That reduces risks like lost data, breaches and bad decisions, and helps the business comply with laws that require keeping and protecting certain records. It can't guarantee profits.

q: Which law requires public companies to keep reliable financial records and internal controls?
e: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act (2002) requires public companies to keep accurate financial records, maintain internal controls over financial reporting and preserve documents, with penalties for destroying records. The other laws cover pollution, wages and trademarks.

q: Using past data to forecast what could happen in the future is
e: Predictive analysis uses historical data and statistical models to forecast future outcomes, such as which customers might close accounts or how much loan demand to expect. Descriptive analysis summarizes what already happened.

q: The first step in developing a project plan is to
o: determine the project's purpose and scope
e: Before buying supplies or assigning tasks, a team must define the project's purpose (why it exists) and scope (what is and isn't included). Every later decision about tasks, budget, schedule and resources depends on that. Unclear scope is a leading cause of project failure.

q: A good project plan acts as a
o: road map that guides the team from start to finish
e: A project plan is a road map: it lays out tasks, timelines, budgets, responsibilities and milestones so the team knows where it's going and can track progress. It guides teamwork but can't guarantee there will be no problems.

q: An employee sees a box blocking a walkway in the bank's storage room. The safest action is to
o: pick it up and put it away
leave it for the cleaning crew
e: The safest action is to remove the hazard right away by picking up the box and putting it away. Slips, trips and falls are among the most common workplace injuries. Stepping over it, leaving it for someone else or waiting to report it leaves the danger in place.

q: Following safety precautions at work mainly reduces the
e: Safety precautions, like keeping walkways clear, using equipment properly and following procedures, reduce the risk of accidents and injuries. That protects employees and lowers costs such as workers' compensation, lost time and lawsuits.

q: After an accident at work, the first step is usually to
o: determine the severity of any injury and get help
clean up before checking on anyone
e: People come first. After an accident, check how badly anyone is hurt and get help, whether first aid, a trained responder or 911 for serious injuries. Paperwork, cleanup and figuring out what happened come after the injured person is cared for.

q: Why should a near-miss accident be reported even though no one was hurt?
o: The next accident could cause an injury
It increases insurance premiums for no reason
e: A near miss reveals a hazard, like a slippery floor or loose shelf, that happened not to hurt anyone this time. Reporting it lets the company fix the problem before the next incident causes a real injury. Many serious accidents are preceded by near misses.

q: Dividing cash-handling duties so one person counts cash and another records deposits helps prevent
e: When one person counts cash and another records deposits, no single employee controls the whole process, so stealing and hiding it would require two people working together. Segregating duties is a basic security precaution against employee theft.

q: Comparing price, quality and delivery terms from several suppliers before choosing one is
e: Bid analysis compares offers from several suppliers on price, quality, delivery time and terms, so the purchaser chooses the best overall value, not just the lowest price. Inventory shrinkage is loss of inventory, and depreciation is an asset's decline in value.

q: How can employees help control a company's expenses?
o: Use supplies carefully and follow cost-saving policies
Order extra supplies just in case
Work more slowly to earn overtime
e: Employees control expenses through everyday habits: using supplies carefully, avoiding waste, protecting equipment and following cost-saving policies. Ordering extras, ignoring procedures or working slowly to earn overtime all raise costs.

q: For many service businesses, the largest expense employees can help control is
e: In service businesses like banks and accounting firms, payroll is usually the largest expense, since the 'product' is people's work. Employees help control it by working productively, managing time well and avoiding unnecessary overtime. Raw materials matter more in manufacturing.

q: Which practice best protects a company's sensitive digital files?
e: Encryption scrambles data so only people with the right key can read it. Even if files are stolen or a laptop is lost, the information stays unreadable. Emailing passwords, using public computers and skipping security updates all expose data.

q: To protect its brand name and logo from being copied, a company should
o: file a patent on its name
e: A trademark legally protects brand names, logos and slogans that identify a company's products, so competitors can't copy them. Patents protect inventions, not names. Registering with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office strengthens that protection.

q: A project manager's key role is to
o: plan the work and mobilize the resources to get it done
e: A project manager plans the work, including tasks, schedule and budget, and mobilizes the people and resources needed to complete it, coordinating the team and communicating with stakeholders. They lead and coordinate rather than doing every task personally.

q: The operations function of a business focuses on
o: transforming resources into goods and services
e: Operations is the function that transforms inputs, such as materials, labor, information and equipment, into the goods and services customers buy. In a bank that means processing transactions and delivering services. Advertising is marketing, and tax law comes from government.

q: Exchanging purchase orders and invoices electronically between companies' computer systems is
e: Electronic data interchange (EDI) lets companies' computer systems exchange business documents like purchase orders and invoices automatically in a standard format, with no paper or retyping. That speeds transactions and reduces errors.

q: Using computer software to plan the materials needed for production is
e: Material requirements planning (MRP) software uses production schedules and inventory levels to calculate which materials are needed, in what quantities and when. That prevents shortages and avoids tying up cash in excess inventory. CRM manages customers, not materials.

q: One of the first steps in planning a project is to
e: Identifying stakeholders, everyone affected by or able to influence the project, is one of the first planning steps, together with defining purpose and scope. Their needs and expectations shape goals, scope and communication. Final reports and closing accounts happen at the end.

q: When evaluating project success, a team should focus on
o: the measures most important to that specific project
only how long the meetings were
e: A project's success should be judged on the measures that matter for that specific project, usually the goals, deadline, budget and quality standards set at the start. Meeting length or another project's metrics don't show whether this project achieved its purpose.

q: An email that looks like it's from a client's bank asks him to 'confirm' his account number and PIN through a link. This scam is called
e: Phishing uses fake emails, texts or websites that imitate trusted companies to trick people into revealing account numbers, passwords or PINs. Real banks never ask for a PIN this way. Front-running and churning are broker abuses, and a margin call is a demand for more collateral in a brokerage account.

q: A freelance graphic designer buys a computer used only for her home-based business. How does tax law usually treat this purchase?
o: It can be deducted as a business expense, lowering taxable income
e: Ordinary and necessary business expenses, including equipment used only for the business, can be deducted (or depreciated) from business income on Schedule C. That lowers taxable profit. A personal-use computer wouldn't qualify, which is why business and personal use should be kept separate.

q: A taxpayer who itemizes donates $2,000 to a qualified 501(c)(3) charity. The main tax effect is that the gift
o: can be deducted, reducing taxable income
is subject to a luxury tax
must be repaid by the charity
e: Cash gifts to qualified charities are deductible for taxpayers who itemize, which lowers taxable income. Starting in 2026, people who take the standard deduction can also deduct up to $1,000 ($2,000 for couples). Keep a written receipt for any single gift of $250 or more.

q: A brokerage that failed to supervise its advisors is ordered by regulators to pay $5 million. This is an example of which consequence of noncompliance?
e: Regulators such as the SEC, FINRA and banking agencies punish compliance failures with fines, plus restrictions and required fixes. Fines are one of the most common consequences, and the public announcement also damages reputation and customer trust.

q: Bank regulators require banks to hold enough capital and follow lending rules mainly to
o: help financial institutions remain stable and prevent failures
set the price of every stock
e: Capital requirements and lending rules make sure banks can absorb losses without failing, which protects depositors and the wider economy. Bank failures can spread panic, as in 2008 and 2023, so stability is a central goal of financial compliance.

q: A compliance officer designs approval steps, access limits and review procedures before a new product launches. She is
o: designing organizational controls to prevent violations
setting interest rates for the Fed
e: A key part of compliance is designing controls, the policies, approvals and procedures that prevent violations before they happen. Building them in before launch is far cheaper than fixing problems later. External audits are done by independent firms after the fact.

q: Compliance software that automatically drives routine checks, such as screening every new customer against sanctions lists, is mainly used for
e: Compliance technology drives or automates routine work, like sanctions screening, transaction monitoring and report generation, so it's done consistently for every customer. That frees compliance staff to investigate real red flags and make judgment calls.

q: How does compliance technology help a company reduce errors?
o: It applies the same rules consistently and removes manual data entry
It removes the need for audits forever
It deletes records after each transaction
e: People get tired and make typing mistakes; software applies rules the same way every time and pulls data directly from systems. That consistency reduces human error in monitoring and reporting. Firms still need training, audits and record-keeping.

q: A bank's compliance dashboard shows that suspicious-activity alerts have doubled at one branch over three months. This shows how technology helps compliance by
o: identifying patterns and trends that need investigation
e: Analytics and dashboards turn large volumes of data into visible trends, like a jump in alerts at one location, so compliance teams know where to look. Spotting patterns early can uncover fraud, weak controls or training gaps before they become major violations.

q: A client says her last advisor rarely returned calls and never explained changes to her portfolio. The main problem in that relationship was
e: Poor communication, like unreturned calls and unexplained changes, is one of the most common reasons clients leave advisors. Finance professionals are responsible for responding promptly and explaining what they do and why. Regular, clear communication builds trust.

q: Clients hire financial professionals largely because the professionals provide
o: expertise and access clients are unable to obtain by themselves
a way to avoid all taxes
e: Clients pay for knowledge, experience and access, such as planning skills, tax strategies and investment options, that they can't easily get on their own. A professional's responsibility is to use that expertise in the client's interest. No one can guarantee returns or eliminate taxes.

q: A bank uses its CRM to chart how a customer's balances and product use have changed over five years to predict future needs. It is analyzing the customer's
e: Looking at how a customer's relationship has moved over time, their trajectory, helps predict what they'll need next, such as a mortgage after years of rising savings. CRM systems store the history that makes this analysis possible.

q: An investor wants to see a company's revenue, expenses and net income for the past year. Which part of the company's filings should she read?
o: The statement of changes in equity
e: The income statement reports revenue, expenses and net income (profit or loss) over a period. Investors use it to judge profitability and growth. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at one date, and the equity statement explains changes in ownership.

q: Where can anyone read a U.S. public company's 10-K, 10-Q and 8-K filings for free?
e: EDGAR, the SEC's Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis and Retrieval system, gives free public access to filings from every U.S. public company, the same primary sources professional analysts use. The other tools serve different purposes: bank lookup, tax filing and dispute records.

q: On a balance sheet, which section shows the owners' claim on the company's assets?
e: Shareholders' equity equals assets minus liabilities, the owners' claim after creditors are paid. Investors watch it to see whether the company is building value. Liabilities are amounts owed to others, receivables are assets, and COGS is on the income statement.

q: A stock table lists: Close 62.50, Net Chg -1.25. Yesterday's closing price was
e: A negative net change means the stock fell from yesterday's close. Add the decline back to today's close: $62.50 + $1.25 = $63.75. Subtracting instead ($61.25) is the common mistake.

q: A stock trades at $48 and its earnings per share are $4. What is its price-earnings (P/E) ratio?
e: P/E = price / earnings per share = $48 / $4 = 12. Investors are paying $12 for every $1 of annual profit. Comparing P/E ratios with similar companies helps judge whether a stock is relatively cheap or expensive.

q: A company's stock jumps 15% in one day on heavy trading volume after it announces a major new contract. This most likely shows that
o: investors are reacting to news about the company
the stock no longer pays dividends
the SEC set a new price
e: Prices and volume in a securities table reflect investor reactions to new information. Good news, like a major contract, raises expected earnings, so buyers bid the price up and trading volume surges. The SEC never sets stock prices.

q: When a bank's customer pays her credit card bill through online bill pay, the bank is performing which role of a financial institution?
o: Making payments on behalf of customers to creditors
e: One role of financial institutions is moving money: making payments for customers through checks, bill pay, ACH and wires. Underwriting is done by investment banks, monetary policy by the Federal Reserve and life insurance by insurers.

q: Before depositing a large sum, a business owner checks whether a bank is well capitalized and FDIC-insured. She is evaluating
o: how risky it is to provide the institution with funds
e: Depositors are lenders to their bank. Checking capital strength, insurance coverage and financial health shows how risky it is to entrust money to that institution, especially for balances above the $250,000 FDIC limit, as SVB depositors learned in 2023.

q: Which market lets companies and governments borrow by issuing debt, and lets investors earn interest by lending?
e: The bond market is where borrowing and lending happen through debt securities: issuers sell bonds to raise money and pay interest to investors. Commodities markets trade raw goods, and forex trades currencies.

q: An investor buys a contract that gives her the right, but not the obligation, to buy a stock at $50 within three months. She bought a(n)
e: An option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a set price before a deadline. Options are derivatives because their value depends on the underlying stock. Bonds, CDs and T-bills are debt instruments.

q: A firm's $90,000 of IT support costs is shared by three departments that use 50%, 30% and 20% of help-desk tickets. How much is allocated to the department using 30%?
e: Allocate the shared cost by the driver: 30% x $90,000 = $27,000. The department using 50% gets $45,000 and the one using 20% gets $18,000, which adds back to $90,000. Allocation divides the cost; it doesn't change the total.

q: Which is the best allocation base for dividing a building's rent among departments?
e: An allocation base should reflect what drives the cost. Rent is paid for space, so square footage is the logical base: a department using a quarter of the floor space bears a quarter of the rent. The other options have no connection to rent.

q: Why do managers allocate indirect costs to products even though the costs can't be traced directly?
o: To know each product's full cost for pricing and profitability decisions
To increase the company's total costs
Because tax law forbids direct costs
e: A product's full cost includes its share of overhead. Without allocation, products look more profitable than they are, and prices may not cover all costs. Allocation spreads the same total cost more realistically; it doesn't increase or avoid it.

q: A financial-information system shows a company's cash, debts and profitability at any moment. This helps managers know the company's
o: financial well-being at any given time
e: Up-to-date financial information gives managers a real-time picture of the company's financial health, such as cash position, obligations and profit, so they can act quickly. Waiting for year-end reports would be too late for many decisions.

q: A main job of financial-information management is to accurately record and report
e: Financial-information management starts with recording and reporting every financial transaction accurately: sales, purchases, payroll and payments. Everything else, including budgets, analysis and decisions, depends on that foundation of accurate data.

q: By analyzing cost data from each department, a manager discovers that one warehouse spends 40% more per order than the others. This shows that financial-information management
o: identifies operational weaknesses and opportunities for improvement
e: Comparing financial data across units reveals where costs are out of line, pointing managers to problems to fix and savings to capture. That's one of the most valuable uses of financial information inside a company.

q: To protect customers' privacy, an ethical company limits which employees can view sensitive financial data. This control is about
e: Limiting access means only employees who need certain data for their job can see it. That protects customer privacy, lowers the risk of identity theft and insider misuse, and is required by privacy and security rules.

q: A company decides how long to keep financial records, where to store them securely and when to destroy them properly. This is part of its
e: Ethical financial-information management includes a storage strategy: keeping records as long as laws require, storing them securely and destroying them safely when no longer needed. Poor storage risks data loss, breaches and legal violations.

q: A bank analyzes a small business's working capital before approving a line of credit. Working capital shows
o: whether the business has enough short-term assets to cover short-term debts
the owner's personal credit score only
e: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities. Positive working capital means the business can likely meet short-term obligations, a key factor for a lender deciding whether a credit line will be repaid.

q: A lender reviews an applicant's credit score mainly to judge the applicant's
e: A credit score summarizes how a person has handled debt, especially payment history and amounts owed. Lenders use it to predict the likelihood of repayment and to set interest rates. Income and job details are checked separately.

q: A company scans its old paper financial records into searchable digital files. This mainly helps it
o: store, retrieve and share records quickly while saving space
eliminate the need to keep records
e: Digital scanning, including digital microfilm scanners for archives, turns paper into searchable files that can be found in seconds, shared securely and backed up. Records still must be kept as long as the law requires.

q: Cloud-based financial systems let a CFO and her team respond quickly to complex questions because they provide
o: up-to-date data that can be queried instantly
e: Modern financial systems store current data in one place and let users run queries and reports instantly, so complex questions get answered in minutes instead of days. They still require strong security.

q: A company uses software to model how taking on a new $2 million loan would affect its future payments and cash flow. This budgeting application is
e: Debt modeling projects how borrowing affects interest, principal payments, cash flow and financial ratios over time. It helps managers decide whether the company can afford the loan before signing.

q: Why does budgeting software increase management's confidence in budgets?
o: It reduces calculation errors and links budgets to actual data
It guarantees budgets will never change
It removes the need for managers
e: Budgeting software automates calculations, pulls in actual results and keeps everyone working from the same numbers, so managers can trust the figures and see variances quickly. That reliability builds confidence in using the budget for decisions.

q: An auditor reviews accounts payable to see whether any vendor shares a phone number or address with an employee. This financial analysis application helps
o: detect fraud such as fake vendors
e: Matching employee data against vendor data in accounts payable is a standard fraud-detection test: a match may reveal an employee who created a fake vendor or secretly owns one. Analytics make it possible to check every vendor quickly.

q: Comparing a company's net profit margin, return on assets and return on equity mainly measures its
e: Net margin, ROA and ROE all measure how well a company turns sales, assets and owners' money into profit, so they're profitability ratios. Liquidity ratios, like the current ratio, measure ability to pay short-term bills.

q: A company tracks the costs of actions it takes to manage climate-related risks, such as flood-proofing facilities, in its reports. This is an example of
o: using financial information in sustainability reporting
e: Sustainability and climate-risk reporting quantify the financial side of environmental issues, such as the cost of protecting facilities or the potential losses from climate events. That's a non-traditional use of financial information.

q: A factory combines Lean methods with Six Sigma. Lean focuses on removing ___, while Six Sigma focuses on improving ___.
e: Lean eliminates waste, steps and inventory that don't add value, while Six Sigma reduces defects and variation to improve quality. Many companies combine them as 'Lean Six Sigma,' using financial data to measure savings.

q: Financial information helps a manufacturer reduce wasted resources because it
o: shows the cost of scrap, rework and idle time so managers can target savings
e: Putting a dollar value on waste, like scrapped materials, rework hours and idle machines, shows managers where the biggest savings are. That's how financial information supports Lean and other efficiency programs.

q: A database automatically records the exact date and time each transaction is entered. This feature, called a date/time stamp, is especially useful for
o: tracking when changes were made and supporting audits
e: Date/time stamps create a reliable record of when each entry or change happened. That supports audit trails, fraud investigations and reconstructing events. Combined with user IDs, it shows who did what and when.

q: An analyst screening thousands of stocks narrows the list by industry, then by country, then by analyst rating. She is using
e: Applying filters one after another narrows a large data set to exactly the records that meet every condition. Filtering by industry, then country, then rating quickly produces a short list. Normalization restructures tables, and Benford's Law tests for fraud.

q: Which finance professional investigates financial records to uncover fraud and may testify in court?
e: Forensic accountants combine accounting and investigative skills to examine records, trace hidden money and uncover fraud, and often serve as expert witnesses. Tellers, agents and loan officers serve customers in day-to-day roles.

q: Besides technical knowledge, which skills do employers in finance say are extremely important?
o: Soft skills such as communication, teamwork and ethics
e: Finance runs on trust and relationships, so employers value soft skills, like clear communication, listening, teamwork, ethics and problem solving, as highly as technical ability. Explaining complex ideas simply to clients is essential.

q: A CFO attends a national finance conference each year. The main professional benefit is that it
o: provides access to valuable industry information and new contacts
replaces the need for a team
e: National conferences bring together experts and peers, giving professionals access to new industry information, trends and best practices, and a chance to build relationships that lead to advice, partnerships and opportunities.

q: A financial advisor stays in touch with her network through regular emails and quick check-in calls, not just when she needs something. This shows that strong professional relationships depend on
e: Professional relationships stay strong through consistent, genuine communication over time. Reaching out only when you want something makes relationships feel one-sided. Regular contact keeps you top of mind for referrals and opportunities.

q: Organizations such as the National Bankers Association and local financial planning societies mainly help finance professionals by
o: providing networking, education and professional support
e: Professional associations connect members through events, mentoring, continuing education and advocacy, which helps them build relationships and careers. They don't set rates, regulate prices or insure deposits; agencies like the Fed and FDIC do that.

q: Corporate governance aligns the interests of
e: Good governance balances the interests of shareholders, managers, employees, customers and the wider community, so the company pursues profit in ways that are responsible and sustainable. That alignment is the core purpose of corporate governance.

q: A company's board adopts strong governance practices mainly to
o: mitigate risk and avoid problems before they occur
e: Governance puts checks in place, including independent oversight, controls and transparency, that reduce the risk of fraud, mismanagement and costly mistakes. Preventing problems is far cheaper than recovering from scandals.

q: In a well-governed company, the board oversees ___ on behalf of ___.
e: The board of directors oversees management on behalf of shareholders and other stakeholders. Directors hire, evaluate and, if needed, replace executives, and approve major decisions. That separation is central to good governance.

q: Policies such as approval limits, reconciliations and segregation of duties that keep a company's operations and reporting reliable are
e: Internal control mechanisms are the policies and procedures a company builds to safeguard assets, ensure accurate reporting and follow laws. They're a core component of a well-governed company. External audits are performed by independent outside firms.

q: A bank uses predictive models that analyze economic data to estimate how many loans might default next year. This shows how technology helps risk management by
o: anticipating risk exposure before losses occur
e: Predictive risk models use historical and current data to estimate future losses, so the bank can set aside reserves, tighten lending standards or adjust prices before problems hit. They improve planning but can't eliminate risk.

q: Which technology risk increases as a company moves more of its operations online?
o: Security risks such as hacking and data breaches
The risk of paper records yellowing
The risk of fewer customers online
e: Digital operations create new security risks: hackers, ransomware and data breaches. That's why companies invest in firewalls, intrusion detection, encryption, backups and employee training as part of risk management.

q: After installing intrusion detection and multifactor authentication, a company's number of successful cyberattacks will most likely
e: Security technology adds layers that block or detect attacks, so successful breaches should decrease. No system eliminates all risk, but layered defenses make attacks much harder and catch intruders faster.

q: In a captive insurance arrangement, the insurance company's policyholders are usually
o: also the owners (stockholders) of the insurance company
e: A captive insurer is owned by the business or businesses it insures, so the policyholders are also its stockholders. That lets them control coverage and keep underwriting profits, while transferring risk away from operating budgets.

q: A company's liability exposure refers to
o: its potential legal responsibility for losses or injuries to others
the amount of cash in its bank account
the number of products it sells
e: Liability exposure is the risk of being held legally responsible for harm to others, such as injuries, damaged property or financial losses. Managing it through safety practices, contracts, warnings and insurance is a key part of legal risk management.

q: Why is staying in compliance with laws and regulations part of managing legal risk?
o: It reduces the chance of fines, lawsuits and sanctions
It lets the company skip insurance
e: Violating laws exposes a company to fines, lawsuits, sanctions and reputational damage. Compliance prevents many of those legal risks, which is why compliance and risk management work closely together.

q: You invest $2,000 at 6% compounded annually. About how much will you have after 2 years?
e: Year 1: $2,000 x 1.06 = $2,120. Year 2: $2,120 x 1.06 = $2,247.20. Simple interest would give $2,240, so the extra $7.20 is interest earned on the first year's interest. Multiply by (1 + rate) once for each year.

q: How much must you invest today at 5% compounded annually to have $11,025 in two years?
e: Present value = FV / (1 + i)^n = $11,025 / (1.05 x 1.05) = $11,025 / 1.1025 = $10,000. Check forward: $10,000 grows to $10,500 after year 1 and $11,025 after year 2.

q: A large financial company that offers banking, insurance, investing and financial planning under one roof is called a
e: A fully integrated financial services provider offers many types of financial products through one company, the result of convergence. Customers get one-stop shopping, and the firm earns more revenue from each relationship.

q: Why do financial companies often earn more after convergence and consolidation?
o: They sell more products to each customer and cut duplicate costs
They eliminate all competition by law
e: Combined firms can cross-sell, offering a bank customer insurance and investments, and eliminate duplicate costs like overlapping branches and systems. Higher revenue per customer plus lower costs often raises earnings.

q: When inflation rises, the purchasing power of money
e: Inflation means prices are rising, so each dollar buys less. That decrease in purchasing power is why investors seek returns above inflation and why rising inflation often leads to higher interest rates that affect financial markets.

q: Strong economic growth, with rising employment and consumer spending, usually affects company earnings and stock prices by
e: In an expanding economy, people earn and spend more, so company sales and profits grow. Higher expected earnings push stock prices up, which is why bull markets usually occur during economic expansions.

q: Compared with investing only at home, investing internationally usually involves
o: higher risk from currency, political and economic differences
e: International investing adds currency risk, political risk and differences in regulation and economic stability. It also adds diversification benefits. Foreign investments aren't FDIC-insured and returns aren't guaranteed.

q: Financial globalization has increased the use of complex instruments, such as currency swaps and futures, that companies use to manage international risk. These instruments are
e: Derivatives get their value from an underlying asset, rate or index, such as an exchange rate. Multinational companies use currency derivatives to hedge against exchange-rate swings as they do business around the world.

q: A corporation issues $500,000 of new common stock. On the statement of changes in equity, this
e: Money raised by selling new shares increases contributed capital, the capital stock part of equity. It isn't revenue because it comes from owners, not customers, and it doesn't affect retained earnings, which change with net income and dividends.

q: A sole proprietor withdraws $8,000 from the business for personal use. On the statement of owner's equity, the withdrawal
o: is recorded as a business expense
e: Owner withdrawals (drawings) take value out of the business, so they reduce owner's equity. They aren't business expenses and don't appear on the income statement, because they're distributions to the owner.

q: The statement of changes in equity connects the income statement and the balance sheet because
o: net income from the income statement flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet
it replaces the cash flow statement
e: Net income for the period is added to retained earnings on the statement of changes in equity, and the ending equity balance then appears on the balance sheet. That's how the financial statements tie together.

q: A manager sets an ambitious but realistic cost target in the production budget so employees have a clear goal to work toward. This shows that cost budgets can
e: Budgets aren't only control tools. They also set targets that motivate employees to work efficiently. Goals that are challenging but achievable work best; impossible targets can push people to cut corners.

q: A cost budget that tells the purchasing department exactly how much it may spend on materials each month is primarily a tool for
e: Cost budgets set spending limits for each area, and comparing actual spending against them keeps finances under control. Overspending shows up quickly as a variance that managers can investigate.

q: When preparing a cost budget, management should consider
o: the business's total cost of production, including materials, labor and overhead
e: A complete cost budget includes direct materials, direct labor and manufacturing overhead, so management sees the full cost of production. Leaving out overhead would understate costs and lead to poor pricing decisions.

q: The chief executive officer can strongly influence a company's governance structure because the CEO
o: leads management and often shapes how decisions are made and reported
e: As the top executive, the CEO shapes company culture, decision-making and how information flows to the board. Whether the CEO also chairs the board is a key governance question. Laws come from Congress and regulators, and audits from independent firms.

q: After a major accounting fraud is discovered, a company is most likely to change its governance structure by
o: adding independent directors and stronger controls
e: Accounting fraud exposes governance weaknesses, so companies usually respond by strengthening oversight with more independent directors, a stronger audit committee, better internal controls and more transparent reporting. Laws like Sarbanes-Oxley came from this kind of response.

q: Who elects a corporation's board of directors, giving them influence over its governance structure?
e: Stockholders (shareholders) own the corporation and vote to elect the board of directors, which then oversees management. Shareholder voting is a key way owners influence governance. Large investors can push for changes through their votes.

q: A manager hires her unqualified relative for a key finance role. Which risk does this unethical choice create?
o: Poor performance, errors and damaged trust among employees
e: Nepotism, hiring a family member who lacks the skills, creates operational risk from mistakes and poor decisions, and damages morale and trust among other employees. Ethical hiring based on qualifications is part of good risk management.

q: A company that uses questionable tactics to boost short-term profits most likely increases its
e: Unethical shortcuts, like misleading customers or cutting safety corners, may raise profits briefly, but they create legal risk (lawsuits and fines) and reputational risk (lost customers and investors) that can far exceed the short-term gain.

q: An employee provides incomplete data to auditors to hide a problem. This is unethical because it
o: prevents the company from seeing and managing a real risk
e: Audits help a company find and fix risks. Hiding information defeats that purpose, lets problems grow and can be illegal. Ethical risk management depends on complete, honest information.

q: A risk that comes from failures in a company's daily processes, systems or people, such as a payment system outage, is a(n)
e: Operational risk arises from breakdowns in internal processes, people or systems, like outages, errors or fraud. Strategic risk relates to competition and long-term direction. ERM tracks both types in one organization-wide view.

q: A company focuses its ERM program on cutting how much a loss costs when it happens, for example by installing sprinklers. This approach is
e: Loss reduction lowers the severity of a loss when it occurs; sprinklers limit fire damage. Loss prevention lowers how often losses happen. Risk avoidance means not doing the activity at all.

q: A project's variance report shows labor hours 25% over budget for three months in a row. Variance analysis like this helps managers
o: identify trends in the data and correct the cause
e: Tracking variances over several periods reveals trends: a one-time spike may be noise, but three straight months over budget signals a real problem, like underestimated hours, that managers should fix.

q: A favorable materials price variance occurs when a company
o: pays less per unit for materials than the standard price
pays more per unit than the standard
e: Price variance compares actual price with standard price. Paying less per unit than standard creates a favorable variance, which helps profit. It's still worth checking that cheaper materials didn't lower quality.

q: Managers analyze variances mainly so they can
o: make appropriate adjustments to operations and future budgets
e: The point of variance analysis is learning: understanding why results differed from plan, then adjusting operations, prices or future budgets. Blame-focused variance analysis discourages honest reporting.

q: Using PIN-based debit transactions and chip cards to protect customers' payments is an example of
o: a risk control that reduces fraud
e: PINs and chip technology make it much harder for criminals to use stolen card information, reducing fraud losses. That's a risk control: it reduces the likelihood of loss without avoiding the activity of card payments.

q: Encryption and secure websites (https) that protect online banking sessions mainly
e: Encryption scrambles data traveling between a customer and the bank, so hackers who intercept it can't read it. Secure connections are a basic risk control for online transactions. Passwords and multifactor authentication are still needed.

q: A company's annual building insurance stays the same no matter how many units it produces. In managerial accounting, this is a
e: Fixed costs, like insurance, rent and salaries, stay the same in total regardless of production volume in the short run. Variable costs, like materials, rise and fall with volume. Knowing which is which is essential for budgeting and break-even analysis.

q: A manager is choosing between keeping an old machine or buying a new one. Which cost should NOT affect the decision?
o: The price paid for the old machine years ago
Future repair costs of the old machine
Future energy savings from the new machine
e: The price paid for the old machine is a sunk cost, already spent and unrecoverable whatever happens now. Only future costs and benefits that differ between options, like the new price, future repairs and energy savings, should drive the decision.

q: A business can rent its spare office space for $1,500 a month but uses it for storage instead. The $1,500 a month is
o: an opportunity cost of using the space for storage
e: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up. By using the space for storage, the business gives up $1,500 of monthly rent it could have earned. That cost doesn't appear in the accounting records but matters for decisions.

q: A store considers adding one more cashier on Saturdays. Marginal analysis would compare
o: the extra sales and customer benefits with the cashier's extra wages
total annual revenue with total rent
last year's profit with this year's taxes
the store's age with its location
e: Marginal analysis looks only at the change a decision causes: the additional revenue (and benefits like shorter lines) from one more cashier versus the additional cost of their wages. If the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost, add the cashier.

q: Producing the 101st unit adds $14 to total cost and $20 to total revenue. Should the company produce it?
o: Yes, because marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost
No, because any added cost lowers profit
Yes, but only if fixed costs rise
No, because revenue is too low
e: The 101st unit adds $20 of revenue and $14 of cost, so profit rises by $6. As long as marginal revenue is at least marginal cost, producing more increases profit.

q: Marginal analysis is most useful for decisions about
o: whether to increase or decrease an activity by a small amount
e: Marginal analysis evaluates incremental changes, like a bit more production, one more employee, an extra hour or a small price change, by comparing their extra benefits and costs. It isn't for recording history or naming a business.

q: Managerial accounting differs from financial accounting because managerial reports
o: can be prepared in any format that helps managers decide
are published in the annual report
e: Managerial reports are for internal use, so they can use any format, level of detail or time period that helps managers decide. Financial accounting reports for outsiders must follow GAAP, and public companies file them with the SEC.

q: A manager asks for a weekly report of each store's labor cost as a percentage of sales. This request is best handled by
e: A custom internal report used to manage operations, like weekly labor cost by store, is a managerial accounting task. Managerial accounting provides timely, detailed information for planning and control.

q: Which question is a managerial accountant most likely to help answer?
o: Should we make this part ourselves or buy it from a supplier?
What was our audited net income last year for investors?
How much tax do we owe the IRS?
What is the national inflation rate?
e: Make-or-buy decisions are classic managerial accounting questions: they compare the relevant costs of each option to support an internal decision. Audited results for investors are financial accounting, and taxes are tax accounting.

q: Inviting employee representatives to share input at certain board meetings helps achieve governance objectives by
o: giving the board front-line insight and building employee commitment
e: Employees see how policies work day to day. Hearing from them gives directors practical insight, and including employees builds commitment to governance goals. The board still makes the decisions.

q: An employee who follows the code of conduct, keeps accurate records and completes compliance training is
e: Governance isn't only the board's job. Every employee supports it by following policies, keeping honest records and staying trained. Those daily actions are what make governance objectives real.

q: Why should employees understand the company's governance objectives?
o: So they know how their actions support ethical, well-run operations
So they can avoid all training
So they can set the stock price
e: When employees understand the purpose behind policies, they're more likely to follow them and to speak up when something seems wrong. Understanding connects individual actions to the company's goals.

q: A board's compensation committee ties executive bonuses to long-term results instead of quarterly profit. This governance process affects management by
o: encouraging decisions that support long-term company health
eliminating the need for a CEO
e: Governance processes shape management behavior. Tying pay to long-term results discourages risky short-term moves, like cutting research or inflating quarterly numbers, and aligns executives with shareholders' long-term interests.

q: Clear governance processes make management decisions more effective because they
o: define who must approve what, so accountability is clear
e: When governance spells out decision rights and approval limits, everyone knows who is responsible for each decision. That speeds routine choices, adds oversight to major ones and makes it clear who's accountable for results.

q: A company's governance policy requires major risks to be reported to the board's risk committee each quarter. This mainly helps the board
o: oversee risk and guide management's decisions
e: Regular risk reporting lets the board oversee the biggest risks and challenge management's plans to handle them. The board guides and oversees; daily operations remain management's job.

q: Changes in customers' buying habits, such as a shift to online shopping, create which type of business risk?
e: When customer preferences shift, a business's sales can fall even if it does nothing wrong. That's market or economic risk, coming from changes in demand. Natural risks come from weather and disasters, and pure hazard risks like fire can only cause loss.

q: An employee keeps work tasks during work hours and personal errands for after work, so neither interferes with the other. This time-management technique is
e: Compartmentalizing means setting aside separate blocks of time and attention for different responsibilities, so commitments don't collide. It helps people focus and meet deadlines. Procrastinating and overcommitting make commitments harder to keep.

q: An advisor presents an investment as having a '90% chance of success' instead of a '10% chance of loss' to make it more appealing. This bias is
e: Framing is presenting the same information in a way that changes how people react. '90% success' sounds better than '10% failure' though they mean the same thing. Ethical advisors present risks honestly and completely so clients can decide fairly.

q: A good information management system makes sure records can be found quickly when needed. This quality is being
e: Information has value only if people can find it when they need it. Retrievable records are organized, indexed and searchable, so employees can answer customers, auditors and regulators quickly. Security matters too, but unreachable records are useless.

q: Employees who complete tasks efficiently with fewer errors help control expenses mainly by
e: Productivity means getting more done with the same resources. Efficient, accurate work reduces rework, wasted materials and overtime, which lowers costs. Ordering extra supplies or ignoring policies raises expenses.

q: A manager gives an employee more responsibility and decision-making authority in her current job to make it more meaningful. This is
e: Job enrichment adds depth: more responsibility, variety and decision-making, which makes work more rewarding and can counter the boredom of narrow specialization. Division of labor and task specialization narrow jobs instead.

q: Workers who perform one very narrow task may lose their jobs when a machine can do that task. This risk of specialization is
e: Job obsolescence happens when a job is no longer needed because technology or process changes replace it. Very specialized tasks are easiest to automate, which is one downside of narrow specialization. Cross-training reduces that risk.

q: A credit card that lets you borrow up to a limit, repay and borrow again is which type of credit?
e: Revolving credit, like credit cards and home equity lines, gives a credit limit you can use, repay and reuse over and over. Installment credit is a fixed amount repaid in set payments, like a car loan or mortgage.

q: When comparing credit cards, which cost is charged every year just for having the card, whether or not you carry a balance?
e: An annual fee is charged yearly simply for having the card, regardless of use. The APR applies only to balances you carry, late fees only if you pay late, and balance transfer fees only when you move debt.

q: For financial information to be useful in decisions, it must be
o: changed each month to look better
e: Managers, lenders and investors can only make good decisions with information that's accurate (reliable) and prepared the same way over time (consistent), so periods can be compared. Exaggerated or manipulated numbers lead to bad decisions.

q: A café owner's financial records show that coffee costs have risen 25% while her prices haven't changed. Using this information, she will most likely
o: raise her prices or find cheaper suppliers
e: Financial information reveals problems like rising costs squeezing profit. Seeing that costs rose while prices stayed flat tells the owner to act by adjusting prices, renegotiating with suppliers or cutting waste. That's exactly why businesses need financial information.

q: Which employee action best helps a bank reach its goal of cutting operating costs by 5%?
o: Turning off unused equipment and reducing paper use
e: Employees help achieve company goals through everyday actions. Turning off unused equipment and cutting paper use directly lower costs. The other actions waste money and work against the goal.

q: A theme park employee learns where every attraction is so she can answer visitors' questions courteously. Her action helps the park
e: Employees contribute to company results when they prepare to serve customers well. Knowing the park lets her give quick, friendly answers, which improves guests' experience and supports the park's goals for satisfaction and repeat visits.

q: After defining a project's purpose and scope, a project team estimates the cost of every task. It is
o: translating the plan into a realistic budget
e: A project plan must include a realistic budget, so the team estimates costs for each task and totals them. That shows whether the project is affordable and gives a standard to track spending against.

q: When developing a project plan, the team lists everything that could go wrong, such as delays or supplier problems. This step is
o: identifying as many known risks as possible
e: Good project plans identify known risks early and plan responses, such as backup suppliers or extra time. That keeps surprises from derailing the schedule and budget.

q: A manufacturer decides whether to make a part itself or buy it from a supplier by comparing its production capabilities with the cost of making the part. This is a decision in
e: Purchasing includes make-or-buy decisions: comparing the cost and capacity to produce an item internally with the cost of buying it. The choice depends on cost, quality, capacity and control.

q: A store buys products from wholesalers to sell to customers at a profit. This type of purchasing is
e: Retailers and wholesalers buy goods for resale, buying products to sell to others at a markup. Industrial purchasing buys materials and equipment used to make products or run a business.

q: Why should a manager recognize that creativity shows up in different ways?
o: People show creativity in a variety of ways, such as solving problems or improving processes
Creativity can't be used in finance
e: Creativity isn't limited to art. In finance it shows up as a new way to solve a client problem, a better process or a clearer presentation. Recognizing different forms of creativity helps managers use everyone's strengths.

q: An analyst adjusts her approach when a client doesn't understand her first explanation and tries a new example. She is showing
o: flexibility, an important part of creativity
e: Flexibility, willingness to change your approach and try new ideas, is a key part of creativity. Finding another way to explain something until it clicks is creative problem-solving in action.

q: Writing down personal goals and reviewing them regularly mainly helps you
o: clarify your goals and stay focused on them
e: Writing goals down clarifies exactly what you want and makes them easier to remember and track. Regular review keeps you focused and lets you adjust. It supports hard work and planning rather than replacing them.

q: Setting clear personal goals contributes most directly to
o: achieving success in life by focusing effort
e: Clear goals focus time and energy on what matters most, which makes success more likely, whether in school, career or finances. They give direction and motivation, the opposite of random decisions.

q: To show the key dates in a client's financial plan, such as the emergency fund by June and a 529 opened in September, the best graphic aid is a
e: A timeline shows events in order along a line of time, so it's ideal for a plan's milestones and deadlines. Pie charts show parts of a whole, scatter plots show relationships between two variables and org charts show reporting structure.

q: A loan officer wants to show customers the steps in the mortgage approval process, from application to closing. The best graphic aid is a
e: A flowchart shows the steps of a process and the order they happen in, with arrows connecting each step. It makes a multi-step process like mortgage approval easy to follow.

q: When meeting a business client from another country, a finance professional should avoid unfamiliar hand gestures mainly because
o: gestures can mean different, even offensive, things in other cultures
all gestures mean the same everywhere
e: Nonverbal signals vary by culture. A gesture that's friendly in one country can be rude in another. Avoiding unfamiliar gestures and learning local customs prevents accidental offense and builds trust.

q: A company entering a new foreign market studies local customs, values and communication styles first. Its main goal is to
o: avoid being insulting or rude and build good relationships
e: Cultural and social environments affect how business is done. Learning local customs helps a company communicate respectfully and avoid mistakes that could insult customers or partners and hurt sales.

q: Taxes charged on specific products such as gasoline and cigarettes are called
e: Excise taxes apply to specific goods, often gasoline, tobacco and alcohol, and are usually included in the price. Income taxes apply to earnings, property taxes to real estate and payroll taxes to wages.

q: The largest source of revenue for the U.S. federal government is the
e: The individual income tax brings in about half of all federal revenue, more than any other source. Payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare are second. Excise taxes, estate taxes and customs duties are much smaller shares.

q: In a team meeting, Jordan calmly says, 'I see it differently, and here's why,' then listens to others. Jordan is being
e: Assertive communication expresses your own views honestly and confidently while respecting others. Jordan disagrees calmly and still listens, the definition of assertiveness. Aggressive behavior disregards others; passive behavior hides your view.

q: Which behavior shows assertiveness when meeting new colleagues?
o: Waiting for others to speak to you first
e: Initiating conversations, introducing yourself and engaging others shows confident, assertive behavior. Waiting silently is passive, and interrupting to talk about yourself is aggressive.

q: The first step in the entrepreneurial process is usually
o: idea generation: identifying a need or want to fill
e: Entrepreneurship starts with idea generation, spotting a need or want that isn't being met and an idea for meeting it. Licensing, hiring and expansion come later, after the idea is tested and the business is planned.

q: Successful entrepreneurs build businesses mainly by
o: creating products or services that meet a need or want
e: Businesses succeed when they meet customers' needs or wants better than alternatives. Entrepreneurs take risks to create those solutions. Avoiding all risk or simply copying competitors rarely builds a lasting business.

q: A start-up founder regularly makes employees work 70-hour weeks without extra pay. Which ethical problem is most likely to hurt the business?
o: Overburdened employees are unlikely to stay with the company
The business will pay fewer taxes
e: Treating employees unfairly by overworking and underpaying them is unethical and drives good people away. High turnover raises hiring and training costs and hurts service. Ethical treatment of employees is part of business ethics in entrepreneurship.

q: Why do customers increasingly expect small businesses to act ethically?
o: Customers want to support companies that share their values and treat people fairly
Laws require customers to check ethics
e: Many customers consider a company's ethics, such as honesty, fair treatment of workers and environmental impact, when deciding where to buy. For small businesses that depend on reputation, ethical behavior builds loyalty and word of mouth.
