q: A bank reviews a company's balance sheet before approving a loan mainly to see
o: its current financial situation: what it owns and owes
e: The balance sheet shows the company's assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time, its current financial situation. Lenders use it to judge whether the company can take on more debt and whether it has assets to support the loan.

q: An accountant refuses a gift from a client whose books she is auditing. She is
o: avoiding a potential conflict of interest
e: Accepting gifts from a client you audit could influence, or appear to influence, your judgment. Refusing protects her independence and objectivity, core ethical standards for accountants.

q: Why must auditors behave independently from the companies they audit?
o: So their opinions on the financial statements are objective and trustworthy
So they can charge higher fees
So companies can choose the results
e: Investors rely on auditors to give an unbiased opinion on whether financial statements are fair. If auditors depend on or favor the client, their opinions lose value. That's why rules limit auditors' financial ties to their clients.

q: When analyzing data, an analyst should make sure the results are
o: unbiased, letting the data speak rather than favoring a desired answer
adjusted to match what her boss wants
based only on data that supports her idea
e: Good data analysis is unbiased: the analyst follows the evidence even if it doesn't support what she expected. Cherry-picking data or shaping results to please someone leads to wrong decisions.

q: A bank studies five years of transaction data to estimate how many customers will apply for mortgages next spring. This type of analysis is
e: Predictive analysis uses historical data to forecast future outcomes, here mortgage demand. Descriptive analysis only summarizes what already happened. Banks use predictions to plan staffing and lending capacity.

q: Joining a local chamber of commerce helps a finance professional's development mainly by
o: providing networking, events and local business knowledge
e: Chambers of commerce connect local business people through events, programs and networking, which builds relationships and market knowledge. They don't replace licenses or guarantee promotions.

q: Many businesses join trade associations partly because the associations help members
e: Trade associations promote their industry, share research and best practices, offer training and advocate on laws affecting members. They can't legally fix prices, and members still compete and follow regulations.

q: Arranging people, tasks and resources so a plan can be carried out is which management function?
e: Organizing comes after planning: deciding who does what, setting up departments, assigning responsibilities and gathering resources. Planning sets goals, and controlling measures results against them.

q: A branch manager checks daily reports, compares them with goals and coaches employees who fall behind. She is mainly performing which management functions?
e: Comparing results with goals is controlling, and guiding and coaching employees is directing (leading). Managers move among planning, organizing, directing and controlling every day.

q: Customs regulations and tariffs on imported goods are often meant to
o: protect a country's economy from foreign competition
e: Customs regulations control what enters a country, and tariffs (customs duties) make imports more expensive, which helps protect domestic businesses from foreign competition. They also collect revenue and enforce safety and security rules.

q: A tax a government collects on goods brought into the country is a
e: A customs duty, or tariff, is a tax on imported goods, collected at the border by customs officials (U.S. Customs and Border Protection). Importers pay it, and the cost is often passed on to buyers.

q: A bank follows not just the exact wording of a consumer-protection law but also its purpose of treating customers fairly. The bank is complying with
o: the spirit as well as the letter of the law
only the letter of the law
e: The letter of the law is its exact wording; the spirit is its intent. Ethical businesses follow both, avoiding technically legal tricks that defeat a law's purpose. Exploiting loopholes may be legal but damages trust.

q: Employees who take part in a lawful public protest should
o: follow laws and avoid violence and vandalism
damage property to make a point
e: Peaceful protest is legal, but violence, vandalism and blocking emergency services are not. Complying with the spirit and intent of laws means expressing views lawfully and respecting others' rights and safety.

q: Effective business writing should be clear and concise so that readers can
e: The goal of business writing is understanding. Clear words, short sentences and logical organization let readers grasp the message quickly and act on it. Long, complicated writing wastes time and causes errors.

q: In a presentation, a speaker's posture, gestures, facial expressions and eye contact are all part of
e: Nonverbal communication is everything you communicate without words: posture, gestures, facial expressions and eye contact. It affects how confident and credible a presenter seems, as in a DECA roleplay.

q: An effective persuasive message to clients should
o: describe the benefits to the audience
focus only on the company's needs
use as much jargon as possible
e: Persuasion works when the audience sees what's in it for them. Explaining benefits, like saving money, reducing risk or reaching goals, motivates action. Persuasive messages usually end with a clear call to action.

q: A student highlights key points, asks questions and summarizes as she reads a long financial report. She is using
e: Active reading means engaging with the text by highlighting, questioning and summarizing, which improves understanding and helps pull out the most relevant information.

q: A report says Company A had 27% market share, Company B 24% and Company C 19%. What is the most relevant fact for an investor comparing market leaders?
o: Company A leads, with B close behind
e: Extracting relevant information means identifying the facts that answer your question. Here, Company A has the largest share (27%) and B is close (24%), the key comparison for judging market leadership.

q: An advisor presenting a retirement plan to a company's board of directors should use a
e: Adapt your style to your audience. A board of directors expects formal, polished, well-organized communication. With a young first-time client, a warmer, simpler style that builds rapport may work better.

q: A professional email signature should include your
o: name, position, company and contact information
home address and Social Security number
e: A professional signature tells recipients who you are and how to reach you: name, title, company and phone or email. Never include sensitive personal information like a Social Security number.

q: An employee needs to discuss a sensitive performance issue with a team member. The best communication channel is
e: Sensitive or personal topics are best handled face to face, privately, where tone and body language help communication and the person can respond. Group emails, texts and public posts can embarrass people and cause misunderstandings.

q: A short internal document that tells employees about a new procedure is usually written as a
e: A memo is a brief internal written message used to share information like new procedures, policies or meeting notices within an organization. Press releases and sales letters go to outside audiences.

q: A report that updates managers on how far a project has advanced and what remains to be done is a
e: A progress report explains what's been completed, what's still left, any problems and whether the project is on schedule and budget. It keeps managers informed so they can make decisions.

q: In a business letter, the inside address and salutation appear
o: before the body of the letter
in the middle of the body
e: Standard business letter format places the date, inside address (recipient's name and address) and salutation ('Dear Ms. Lee:') before the body, then the closing and signature after it.

q: A good business letter gets to the point without unnecessary words. This quality is
e: Conciseness means saying what you need in as few words as possible without losing clarity. Busy readers appreciate letters that get to the point. Wordy or vague letters waste time and may be misunderstood.

q: Turning a dense table of investment returns into an infographic is likely to make readers
o: pay more attention and understand the data faster
e: Data visualization, like infographics, charts and heat maps, makes information easier to grasp and more engaging, so audiences pay more attention and remember it. That's why charts help in roleplays.

q: Which action best builds positive customer relations when a client explains a problem?
o: Finish their sentences to save time
e: Positive customer relations start with respectful listening. Letting customers explain fully shows you value them and helps you understand the real problem. Interrupting, being distracted or arguing damages the relationship.

q: Positive customer relations benefit a business partly by
o: avoiding wasted time and resources spent on complaints and lost customers
e: Good customer relations prevent many problems, so fewer complaints, refunds and lost customers save time and money. Keeping existing customers is also far cheaper than finding new ones.

q: A bank teller explains to a customer why a deposit hold policy exists. Clear explanations of business policies help customers
e: When employees explain the reason behind a policy, such as holds protecting against bad checks, customers are more likely to understand and accept it. Unexplained rules feel arbitrary and frustrate customers.

q: A customer seems suspicious and questions every fee. The employee should
o: stay patient, explain clearly and provide documentation
e: Difficult customers, including suspicious ones, can be any age or background. Patience, clear explanations and written documentation build trust and resolve concerns. Getting defensive or refusing to answer makes them more suspicious.

q: Strong customer relationship management usually leads to greater
e: CRM focuses on understanding and serving customers well over time, which builds loyalty, so customers stay longer and buy more. Loyal customers cost less to keep than new ones cost to win.

q: Satisfied, loyal customers often recommend a business to friends and family. This benefit of CRM is
e: Happy customers become advocates, sharing positive experiences with others. That word-of-mouth promotion is free, trusted marketing, and it's one of the biggest benefits of strong customer relationships.

q: When meeting clients from other cultures, a simple way to show respect is to
o: learn to pronounce their names correctly
e: Pronouncing someone's name correctly shows respect and care, building trust from the start. Asking politely how to say a name is better than guessing or using a nickname they didn't choose.

q: The economic activity of creating goods and services is called
e: Production is creating goods and services. Consumption is using them, and distribution is moving them to customers. All three are basic economic activities.

q: Which is an example of a capital resource used to produce goods and services?
o: A highway used to transport goods
e: Capital resources are human-made tools and structures used in production: highways, buildings, machinery and equipment. A lake is a natural (land) resource, skills are labor and ideas are entrepreneurship.

q: A hurricane destroys much of the region's orange crop. According to supply and demand, this natural disaster will most likely
e: Natural disasters can sharply cut supply. With fewer oranges available and demand about the same, prices rise. Supply and demand explain how events like disasters affect prices.

q: Laws that set minimum safety standards in factories are an example of government
e: The government regulates business to protect workers, consumers and the public. Workplace safety laws, enforced by OSHA, are a common example. In a market economy, the government regulates but doesn't own most businesses or set prices.

q: When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it must
o: increase borrowing by issuing Treasury securities
e: A budget deficit means spending exceeds revenue, so the federal government borrows by selling Treasury bills, notes and bonds. That borrowing adds to the national debt and can affect interest rates for businesses.

q: A business's main reason for operating is to
o: make a profit by meeting customer needs
e: For-profit businesses exist to earn a profit by providing goods and services customers want. Profit rewards owners for taking risk and funds growth. Factors like costs, prices and competition all affect it.

q: Hotels in a city offer special weekend room rates to attract travelers away from rivals. This is an example of
e: Competition is rivalry among businesses for customers, often through prices, quality and service. Special rates to win travelers from other hotels show competition benefiting consumers. Price fixing would be an illegal agreement among rivals.

q: A bank measures how many loan applications each employee processes per day. It is measuring
e: Productivity is output per unit of input, such as loan applications processed per employee per day. Higher productivity lowers costs per unit and raises profit. Inflation, market share and GDP measure other things.

q: A company improves training, equipment and the work environment so employees can do more in less time. This improves both productivity and employees'
e: Better tools, training and working conditions improve quality of work life, which also tends to raise productivity because satisfied, well-equipped employees work more effectively.

q: Reducing government purchases, with everything else unchanged, would directly cause GDP to
e: GDP = consumer spending + business investment + government purchases + net exports. Cutting government purchases lowers one component, so GDP decreases unless other spending rises to offset it.

q: A factory adds more and more workers to the same machines, and eventually each new worker adds less output than the one before. This illustrates
e: The law of diminishing returns says that adding more of one input to a fixed amount of another eventually yields smaller increases in output, as workers get in each other's way. It explains why costs per unit can start rising.

q: If adding one more worker actually reduces total output because of crowding, the worker's marginal return is
e: When an added input lowers total output, its marginal return is negative. That's the extreme end of diminishing returns, a sign the business has more of that input than its fixed resources can use.

q: Promoting, pricing and distributing products to customers are which type of business activity?
e: Marketing activities include product planning, pricing, promotion, distribution and selling, everything involved in getting products to customers. Production creates them, and finance and accounting manage money.

q: Evaluating a company's ratios to decide whether it can afford to expand is part of which business activity?
e: Finance manages money: obtaining funds, investing them and analyzing financial performance. Financial analysis of whether the company can afford expansion is a finance activity.

q: A company that cuts corners on safety to save money most directly increases its
o: financial risk from lawsuits, fines and lost sales
e: Unethical choices create financial risk: lawsuits, regulatory fines, recalls and lost customers can cost far more than the money saved. Business ethics and financial health are closely linked.

q: When no specific rule covers a situation, an employee's decision about what's right is guided mainly by
e: A personal code of ethics, an individual's values and principles about right and wrong, guides behavior when laws or policies don't give a clear answer. Companies also provide codes of conduct to support ethical decisions.

q: A bank's procedures change overnight because of a new regulation. An adaptable employee will
o: adjust to the new situation and learn the new steps
refuse to follow the new procedures
complain until the rules change back
e: Adaptability means adjusting quickly and positively when circumstances change. In finance, rules, technology and markets change often, so adaptable employees are highly valued.

q: Volunteering to learn a new software system that intimidates you shows you are
o: willing to leave your comfort zone
e: Adaptable people are willing to step outside their comfort zone to learn and grow. Taking on something unfamiliar builds skills and confidence and shows employers you can handle change.

q: Two departments disagree over a shared budget, and their managers meet to work out a compromise that gives each part of what it wants. They are
e: Negotiating is a conflict-resolution skill in which parties discuss their interests and reach an agreement both can accept, often through compromise. Avoiding ignores the conflict, and forcing imposes one side's will.

q: People with healthy self-esteem generally see themselves as
e: Self-esteem is how you value yourself. Healthy self-esteem means seeing yourself as worthy and capable while staying realistic, not arrogant. It supports confidence, resilience and good relationships.

q: Which experience most often builds self-esteem?
o: Achieving a goal you worked hard for
e: Achievement, setting a goal, working for it and succeeding, is a powerful builder of self-esteem because it proves your abilities to yourself. Constant criticism and comparison tend to lower self-esteem.

q: A responsible employee balances her own needs with those of others by
o: completing her work reliably while helping teammates when they need it
e: Responsible behavior means being dependable and accountable while considering others: doing your share, meeting commitments and supporting the team. Self-centered behavior, missed deadlines and taking credit undermine trust.

q: An employee admits she forgot to file a report and stays late to finish it. She is demonstrating
e: Responsibility means owning your duties and mistakes and fixing them. Admitting the error and finishing the work shows accountability, which builds trust with managers and teammates.

q: Which habit can help someone feel more self-confident before an important presentation?
o: Preparing thoroughly and dressing in professional clothes that feel good
e: Confidence grows from preparation and from small things that help you feel ready, like professional clothing that fits well. Practicing builds competence, and competence builds confidence.

q: An employee who finishes her assignments and asks her manager for additional work is showing
e: Initiative means taking action without being told, such as seeking more responsibility, offering ideas or solving problems proactively. Employees with initiative stand out and are often considered for promotions.

q: Employees who adjust well to change at work often
o: make positive changes of their own
e: People who handle change well see it as unavoidable and look for opportunities in it, often suggesting improvements themselves. Resisting or waiting for things to go back makes adjusting harder.

q: A person who sets high standards, takes calculated risks and persists toward goals shows
e: Achievement orientation is a drive to set challenging goals, work toward excellence and persist through obstacles. It's often linked with an entrepreneurial spirit and leadership.

q: An employee with strong achievement orientation is most likely to
o: seek challenging goals and lead efforts to meet them
wait to be told what to do
e: People driven to achieve take on challenging goals, often stepping into leadership roles to accomplish them. They measure themselves by results and keep improving, unlike those who do the minimum.

q: A financial advisor says, 'I can see this decision is stressful for you,' before discussing options. She is showing
e: Empathy means understanding and acknowledging another person's feelings. Recognizing a client's stress before moving to solutions makes them feel heard and builds trust.

q: A manager who makes every decision alone and expects employees to obey without input has which leadership style?
e: Authoritarian (autocratic) leaders make decisions alone and expect compliance. It can work in emergencies but often hurts morale and working relationships. Democratic leaders involve the team; laissez-faire leaders give it free rein.

q: The foundation of positive working relationships is mutual
e: Positive working relationships rest on mutual respect: valuing others' ideas, time and contributions. Respect leads to trust, better communication and more effective teamwork.

q: Employees who work on effective teams often report higher
e: Being part of a supportive, effective team gives people a sense of belonging, shared success and help when needed, which raises job satisfaction and engagement.

q: A small group of employees meets regularly to find and solve work-quality problems. This is a
e: A quality circle is a small team of employees who meet regularly to identify, analyze and solve quality problems in their work area. It uses front-line knowledge and builds teamwork.

q: An employee is bored with routine tasks. A manager motivates him by
o: giving him a new, challenging project
e: Many people are motivated by challenge, growth and meaningful work. A new, challenging project can renew engagement. Ignoring boredom or reducing responsibilities usually lowers motivation further.

q: According to motivation theory, once a need such as fair pay is satisfied, it
o: no longer motivates much, so other factors like recognition and growth matter more
becomes the only thing employees care about
e: Satisfied needs stop driving behavior strongly (as in Maslow's hierarchy and Herzberg's theory). Once pay feels fair, people are motivated more by recognition, achievement, responsibility and growth.

q: An effective shared vision for a team should be
o: clear enough to be summed up concisely
e: A good vision is clear, memorable and concise, so everyone understands and can repeat it. That clarity aligns people's efforts. A vision no one can remember or understand can't guide a team.

q: Why does a shared vision help a team?
o: It focuses team members' energy on common goals
It removes the need for communication
e: A shared vision gives everyone a common direction, so effort goes toward the same goals instead of competing priorities. It also motivates people by connecting their work to something meaningful.

q: After a client complains, an advisor says, 'That was my decision, and I'll fix it.' He is
e: Taking responsibility means owning your decisions and their results, especially when things go wrong. That builds trust and credibility. Blaming others damages relationships and reputation.

q: Which behavior shows a failure to take responsibility?
o: Blaming a coworker for your own mistake
Admitting an error and correcting it
e: Blaming others for your own mistakes avoids accountability and damages trust. Responsible people admit errors, fix them, ask for help when needed and keep their promises.

q: A new analyst is given an assignment with incomplete information and stays calm while working through it. She is showing
e: Tolerance for ambiguity is the ability to stay calm and productive when information is unclear or incomplete. In finance, decisions often must be made without perfect information.

q: Having strong moral principles and sticking to them even when it's difficult is called
e: Integrity means being honest and consistent with your values even under pressure. An ethical dilemma is a situation where values conflict, and integrity helps you choose the right action.

q: A manager who applies the same attendance rules to every employee, including friends, is being
e: Fairness means treating people consistently, using the same standards for everyone regardless of personal relationships. Inconsistent treatment damages trust and morale and can create legal risk.

q: People feel they are being treated fairly when they believe they
o: are being treated the way they deserve to be treated
e: Perceived fairness comes from believing that treatment matches what you've earned or deserve, with consistent rules and honest processes. Fairness isn't getting everything you want; it's being treated justly.

q: A coworker always delivers her part of a project on time and as promised. Her teammates trust her because of her
e: Trust grows from dependability: consistently doing what you said you'd do. Popularity or position doesn't build lasting trust; reliable behavior over time does.

q: When leaders consistently act ethically, employees are more likely to
o: support the organization's mission and behave ethically too
e: Leaders set the tone. When they model ethical behavior, employees see that values matter, trust leadership more and are more motivated to support the mission and act ethically themselves.

q: Holding yourself to the same rules you expect of others and accepting consequences for your actions demonstrates
e: Accountability means taking ownership of your actions and their results and holding yourself to the same standards as others. It's essential to modeling ethical behavior.

q: A team agrees with a flawed plan because no one wants to disagree, and the plan fails. This is an example of
e: Groupthink happens when the desire for harmony leads a group to accept ideas without critical evaluation. Challenging the status quo and inviting dissent helps teams avoid it.

q: Taking time to understand viewpoints that conflict with your own can lead to
e: Considering opposing views exposes you to new information and helps you communicate more effectively. Decisions improve because more perspectives are weighed.

q: Listening carefully to a colleague's opposing argument helps you become more
e: Understanding why someone disagrees helps you see things from their perspective, which builds empathy. Empathy improves relationships and makes it easier to find solutions everyone can accept.

q: A manager treats two employees differently in the same situation because she likes one more. This mainly shows a failure to consider
o: fairness and the long-term impact of actions on others
e: Treating people differently in the same situation is unfair and can damage trust, morale and relationships over time. Considering the long-term impact of actions on others means applying consistent standards.

q: An employee decides before acting without understanding all the facts, causing problems for others. This gap in understanding is a
e: A knowledge gap is missing information needed for a good decision. Acting without closing it can harm others. Assessing the long-term impact of actions means getting the facts first.

q: Bitcoin and Ethereum are examples of
e: Cryptocurrencies are digital currencies that run on decentralized blockchain networks and aren't issued by governments. Federal Reserve notes are U.S. paper currency, and Treasury bonds and notes are government debt.

q: A shopper uses money to buy groceries instead of trading something for them. This shows money's function as a
e: As a medium of exchange, money is accepted in trade for goods and services, which avoids the inefficiency of barter. Store of value and unit of measure are money's other main functions.

q: Accounting software that automatically calculates employees' pay, taxes and deductions helps a business
e: Accounting technology automates payroll: calculating wages, withholding taxes and benefits, and creating pay stubs and tax forms. That saves time and reduces errors, though the business still owes the taxes.

q: Businesses must keep accurate accounting records partly because of legal requirements for
e: Tax laws require businesses to keep records that support the income, expenses and deductions they report. Inaccurate records can bring IRS penalties. That's a key legal consideration in accounting.

q: Managing a company's cash, inventory, receivables and short-term debts so it can pay bills on time is
e: Working capital management, part of the finance function, balances current assets and current liabilities so the business has enough cash for daily operations without leaving too much money idle.

q: An employee secretly takes company funds for personal use. This crime is
e: Embezzlement is stealing money or property entrusted to you by your employer. It's a serious crime and a key legal consideration in finance, prevented with internal controls like segregation of duties.

q: Which is a liability that reduces a young graduate's net worth?
e: Liabilities are debts you owe, and student loans are a common large liability for young adults. Savings, retirement accounts and a paid-off car are assets, which increase net worth.

q: An ethical human resources department ensures fairness by
o: using the same hiring process for all applicants
e: Using a consistent hiring process, with the same job criteria, questions and evaluation for everyone, keeps decisions fair, reduces bias and lowers the risk of discrimination claims. HR also makes sure the company's ethics code is followed.

q: Marketing helps companies in a global economy mainly by
o: creating a competitive advantage by understanding and meeting customer needs
e: Marketing identifies what customers want and how to reach them, which helps a company stand out from competitors at home and abroad. It also supports trade by connecting products with markets around the world.

q: An employee needs to discuss a complicated, sensitive issue with her boss. Instead of a long email, she should
o: talk to her boss in person
post it in a group chat
e: Email works well for routine information, but complicated or sensitive issues are better discussed in person, where tone is clear and questions can be answered immediately.

q: To remember to respond to an important email later, a user can
e: Most email programs let users flag or star messages for follow-up, which keeps important tasks visible. Deleting or marking as spam risks losing it, and forwarding to everyone clutters other inboxes without getting the reply done.

q: A bank's website tracks which pages visitors click and how long they stay. This internal record is
e: Clickstream data records a visitor's path through a website: pages viewed, clicks and time spent. Businesses use it to understand customer interests and improve websites and marketing.

q: The unique web address customers type to reach a business's website, such as examplebank.com, is its
e: A domain name is the human-readable address of a website. Businesses register domain names that match their brand so customers can find them easily. Behind the scenes, the domain points to the server's numeric IP address.

q: Before creating a business website, a company usually must first register
e: Registering a domain name secures the business's web address through a registrar. Then the business sets up hosting and builds the site. Patents and stock offerings aren't required for a website.

q: Using another company's photos on your website without permission may violate
e: Copyright protects original works like photos, text and videos. Using them without permission or a license can lead to legal action. Information management must follow intellectual property laws.

q: A customer wants to know a bank's current CD rates. The fastest, most reliable way is to
o: ask a random social media group
e: Obtaining information efficiently means going to the most direct, reliable source. The bank's official website lists current rates. Social media posts may be outdated or wrong.

q: To store digital files for future use, an employee should
o: create an organized system and keep only what's needed
save everything on the desktop with random names
e: Effective storage means an organized folder system with clear names, keeping what's needed and deleting what isn't, so files are easy to find later. Random names and cluttered desktops waste time.

q: Saving a frequently used website in your browser so you can return to it quickly is called
e: Bookmarking saves a web page's address in your browser for quick access later, a simple way to store information you'll need again. Encrypting protects data, and normalizing and filtering are database techniques.

q: Software such as Windows or macOS that manages a computer's hardware and runs other programs is the
e: The operating system manages hardware like memory, storage and devices, and provides the platform other programs run on. Spreadsheets, databases and browsers are applications that run on top of it.

q: Keeping a computer's operating system updated is important mainly because updates
o: fix security weaknesses and improve performance
e: Operating system updates patch security holes hackers could exploit and fix bugs. Delaying updates leaves systems vulnerable, which is a serious risk for financial businesses.

q: A business that relies heavily on machinery and equipment rather than human labor is described as
e: Capital-intensive production uses a large investment in machinery and equipment relative to labor, like auto plants. Labor-intensive production relies mainly on people, like many service businesses.

q: A crucial element of a quality culture is
o: training employees thoroughly so they can do their jobs right
e: Quality cultures invest in thorough training so employees know standards and how to meet them, and leaders encourage reporting problems. Quality is built in, not inspected in after complaints.

q: Quality is often built into a product most effectively during
e: Designing quality in from the start, with clear specifications, testing and reliable processes, prevents defects more cheaply than catching them later. That's why quality control begins in design.

q: A project manager notices her team is stressed and falling behind. A good corrective action is to
o: motivate them by reducing stress and building confidence
add more pressure and longer hours
e: Monitoring projects includes the people side. Addressing stress, by clarifying priorities, adjusting workloads and recognizing progress, helps the team regain confidence and get back on schedule.

q: A job posting that says 'Full-time manager needed immediately' tells a job seeker the employer
o: wants to fill the position quickly
e: Reading job postings carefully shows what the employer needs and how urgently. 'Needed immediately' signals a quick hiring process, so qualified applicants should apply promptly.

q: A business that matches job seekers with employers, sometimes charging a fee, is a
e: Private employment agencies help connect job seekers with employers, often charging the employer (sometimes the applicant) a fee. Using several job-search strategies increases your chances.

q: A follow-up letter after a job interview can be used to
o: thank the interviewer and provide further information
ask for a higher salary before an offer
e: A follow-up letter thanks the interviewer, restates your interest and can add information you forgot or reinforce key qualifications. It should be polite and sent after every interview.

q: Which trait is common among successful entrepreneurs?
e: Successful entrepreneurs tend to be optimistic, confident that challenges can be overcome. Combined with persistence and a willingness to take calculated risks, optimism helps them push through setbacks.

q: What is the difference between entrepreneurial skills and traits?
o: Skills are learned through training; traits are repeated behaviors that become part of personality
Traits are taught in classes only
e: Skills, such as budgeting, marketing and planning, can be learned and practiced. Traits, such as optimism, persistence and creativity, are patterns of behavior that become part of who you are, though they can also develop over time.

q: When working with a team to solve a problem, it's important to
o: dismiss ideas that differ from yours
e: Respecting different opinions encourages people to share ideas, which leads to better solutions. Teams that dismiss differing views miss options and damage relationships.

q: An employee who regularly goes over his supervisor's head may find that
o: other employees may not trust him
e: Bypassing the chain of command damages relationships with your supervisor and coworkers and can make you seem untrustworthy. It also skips the person responsible for daily operations who could solve the problem.

q: Employees help their organization meet its goals mainly by
o: doing their jobs well and supporting the business's priorities
e: Organizational goals are reached through employees' daily work. When employees understand priorities and perform their roles well, the business achieves its goals.

q: Managers help employees contribute to organizational goals by
e: Employees can only support goals they understand. Managers who clearly communicate priorities and how each role contributes help everyone focus on what matters most.

q: A company planning a concert decides to hire a different band because the first one has a history of canceling. This risk-management choice is
e: Choosing a more reliable band removes the specific risk of a cancellation by that band, which is risk avoidance. Buying event insurance would transfer risk, and keeping the first band would retain it.

q: Patents, trademarks and copyrights are legal tools that protect
e: Intellectual property is creations of the mind: inventions (patents), brand names and logos (trademarks), and creative works (copyrights). Legal protection lets creators benefit from their work and stops others from copying it.

q: A competitor spreads false statements claiming a bank is going bankrupt, causing customers to leave. This tort is
e: Defamation is a tort (civil wrong) in which false statements damage someone's reputation, slander if spoken and libel if written. The bank could sue for damages.

q: A debtor who chooses to file for bankruptcy is using which type of bankruptcy filing?
e: In a voluntary bankruptcy the debtor chooses to file for court protection. In an involuntary bankruptcy creditors petition the court to force the debtor into bankruptcy.

q: When writing an inquiry letter or email asking for information, you should include
o: your contact information so the reader can respond
no details about what you need
a demand for an instant reply
e: An effective inquiry clearly states what you need and why, and includes your contact information so the recipient can respond easily. Without it, the reader may not be able to reply at all.

q: A client asks a complicated question during a meeting. The advisor should
o: ask for clarity if needed and make sure to answer the question fully
e: Legitimate responses address what was actually asked. Asking clarifying questions ensures you understand, and answering fully builds trust. If you don't know, say so and commit to follow up by a specific time.

q: Which technique encourages a speaker during a conversation?
o: Nodding, smiling and maintaining eye contact
e: Supportive nonverbal cues, like nodding, smiling and eye contact, show you're listening and engaged, which encourages the speaker to continue. Distraction and negative body language discourage them.

q: When giving verbal directions to a new employee, you should
e: Clear verbal directions use specific steps and concrete examples, so the listener knows exactly what to do. Vague or rushed directions lead to mistakes.

q: A note-taking method that organizes main ideas and supporting details in a structured list is
e: Outlining arranges notes hierarchically, with main points and indented details, showing how ideas relate. It's efficient and makes review easier. Transcribing every word is slow and makes the key points harder to spot.

q: Choosing an appropriate format for professional writing, such as headings and bullet points, helps
o: organize content in a cohesive, manageable way
e: Good formatting, with headings, sections, bullets and white space, organizes content so readers can follow and find information quickly. Format should fit the document's purpose and audience.

q: Why is it recommended to smile when answering a business phone call?
o: Smiling makes your voice sound friendlier
e: Callers can hear a smile: it changes your tone and makes you sound warmer and more welcoming. Professional phone etiquette also includes greeting callers, identifying yourself and listening carefully.

q: After receiving oral directions, restating them in your own words helps
o: confirm and clarify that you understood correctly
e: Paraphrasing directions back to the speaker confirms you understood and gives them a chance to correct mistakes before you start, which prevents costly errors.

q: An insurance agent calls a client a week after a policy starts to make sure she's satisfied with her coverage. This shows
e: A customer service mindset focuses on meeting customer needs beyond the sale. Following up to confirm satisfaction shows care, catches problems early and builds loyalty.

q: Businesses contribute to society mainly by
o: providing goods, services and jobs, and paying taxes
e: Businesses play a central role in society: they produce goods and services people need, create jobs and income, pay taxes that fund public services and drive innovation.

q: Economists closely watch consumer spending as an economic indicator because
o: it makes up about two-thirds of U.S. GDP
e: Consumer spending makes up about 68% of U.S. GDP, so changes in how much people spend strongly signal whether the economy is growing or slowing. Retail sales and consumer confidence reports are closely watched.

q: When a company opens factories abroad to reach new markets and lower costs, it is most likely aiming for
o: increased production and sales in the global environment
e: Operating globally lets companies tap new customers, resources and lower-cost production, increasing output and sales. It also brings risks like currency swings and political uncertainty.

q: Companies adapt to fast-changing markets by adopting new technology mainly to achieve
e: New technology helps companies produce more with less, respond faster and serve customers better, which raises productivity and keeps them competitive. Companies that don't adapt often lose market share.

q: Learning a few phrases of a foreign business partner's language mainly
o: shows respect and can improve business relations
e: Making an effort to use a partner's language signals respect and interest in their culture, which builds goodwill and trust. Professional interpreters may still be needed for important negotiations.

q: Which geographic feature most helps a country participate in world trade?
o: A long coastline with good ports
e: Coastlines with deep-water ports make shipping goods cheaper and easier, which encourages trade. Landlocked or isolated countries face higher transportation costs.

q: Which document is required for most international business travel?
e: A valid passport is required for nearly all international travel. Some countries also require visas, proof of immunizations or sponsorship letters, so business travelers should check requirements early.

q: When assessing your strengths and weaknesses honestly, one helpful approach is to
o: identify a strength for every weakness
e: Balancing self-assessment by pairing each weakness with a strength keeps it honest but positive. Feedback from others gives a more accurate picture, since people often misjudge their own strengths and weaknesses.

q: When speaking, which vocal habit shows interest and enthusiasm?
e: Varying pitch, tone and pace makes your voice engaging and shows enthusiasm. A monotone sounds bored and loses listeners' attention, which matters in roleplays and presentations.

q: A coworker leaves a personal letter on her desk. Respecting her privacy means you should
e: Respecting privacy means not intruding into others' personal information or belongings without permission. Reading or sharing someone's personal letter violates their trust.

q: When coaching a team member, the most useful feedback is
e: Effective coaching gives specific, constructive feedback about what to keep doing and what to improve, delivered respectfully. Vague criticism or silence doesn't help people grow.

q: Convincing your parents to start giving you and your siblings a weekly allowance by explaining how it will teach money management is an example of
e: Selling an idea means persuading others by showing how it benefits them, here teaching money skills. It's the same skill used in a roleplay when you persuade a judge to accept your recommendation.

q: Which statement about ethics is true?
o: Unethical actions are not always illegal
Ethics and laws are exactly the same
e: Laws set minimum standards, but ethics goes further. Some actions, like misleading a client while technically following disclosure rules, may be legal but still unethical.

q: When facing an ethical dilemma, a good first question to ask is
e: Recognizing an ethical dilemma starts with asking whether ethical principles like honesty, fairness or responsibility are at stake. Then you can consider options, consequences and who's affected.

q: Someone who chooses jobs that involve lots of teamwork and client contact might place a high value on
e: Your values, what matters most to you, shape your choices. Preferring teamwork and client contact suggests valuing social interaction, which fits careers like financial planning and relationship banking.

q: A manager shares the real reasons behind a difficult decision with her team. She is
o: being transparent and fostering honest communication
e: Transparency means openly sharing information and reasoning, even about difficult topics. It builds trust and reduces rumors and confusion, because people accept hard decisions more readily when they understand why.

q: Comparing your checkbook register with your bank statement and resolving differences is called
e: Reconciling means matching your records to the bank statement, accounting for outstanding checks, deposits in transit, fees and interest. It catches errors and fraud early.

q: A financial institution that offers checking, savings and loans to individual consumers is a
e: Retail (consumer) banks serve individuals with checking, savings, credit cards and personal loans. Investment banks help companies raise capital, and central banks like the Fed manage monetary policy.

q: On a check, the line labeled 'Pay to the order of' is where you write
e: 'Pay to the order of' identifies the payee, the person or business receiving the money. The amount goes in the box and on the written line, and your signature goes on the bottom line.

q: Business records are best described as
o: official, documented evidence of a company's transactions and activities
e: Business records, such as invoices, receipts, contracts and financial statements, document a company's transactions and activities. They support decisions, taxes, audits and legal compliance.

q: A digital app that lists your tasks, deadlines and reminders is an
e: Electronic task organizers (to-do list apps) help people manage tasks and deadlines with reminders and priorities, a personal productivity tool. An operating system runs the computer itself.

q: To return quickly to useful research websites later, a student can use
e: Browser bookmarks save web addresses for easy access, an efficient web-search skill. They can be organized into folders by topic, so a student can jump back to trusted sources instead of searching again.

q: When naming a word-processing file, which name follows a clear, consistent convention?
e: Clear file names describe the content and include a date, making files easy to find and sort. Vague names like 'stuff' or 'final final' cause confusion.

q: The computer memory that temporarily holds data and programs while they're being used is
e: RAM is fast, temporary memory that holds data the computer is actively using. It's cleared when the power is off, unlike storage drives that keep data permanently.

q: Information management in a company should follow clear standards mainly so that employees handle data
e: Ethics in information management means collecting, using and sharing data honestly, protecting privacy and keeping it accurate. Clear standards guide employees to do that consistently.

q: A team writing a client proposal together uses file-sharing software so everyone edits the same document. This helps them
o: collaborate and create a common voice
e: Shared documents let team members contribute, comment and edit in one place, keeping one current version and a consistent voice. Emailing separate copies creates confusion.

q: The first step in identifying resources needed for a project is
o: gaining a clear understanding of what is needed
e: Before gathering people, money and materials, you must understand the project's requirements. That clarity prevents over- or under-spending and delays.

q: When should you read the instructions for a new piece of equipment?
o: Before using the equipment for the first time
e: Reading instructions before first use helps you operate equipment safely and correctly, preventing injuries and damage. Waiting until it breaks, or relying on a coworker's memory, risks accidents and costly repairs.

q: A written document that tells employees what to do during a fire, storm or medical emergency is
e: An emergency plan explains evacuation routes, who to call, where to meet and each person's responsibilities, so employees respond quickly and safely instead of panicking.

q: An arrangement in which a supplier automatically ships the same items on a regular schedule is a
e: A standing order delivers set items at regular intervals without reordering each time, saving time for routine supplies. A back order means an item is out of stock, and a rush order speeds one delivery.

q: When evaluating a project's results, a team should
o: evaluate its successes and obstacles to learn for next time
e: A project review examines what went well and what didn't, so lessons improve future projects. Focusing only on blame or skipping the review wastes that learning.

q: The main purpose of quality control methods at work is
e: Quality control methods, like checklists, inspections and testing, catch and prevent errors before products or services reach customers, protecting satisfaction and reducing costly rework.

q: Which unethical operations practice might a company use to reduce its tax bill improperly?
o: Underreporting production or sales so it pays fewer taxes
e: Falsifying operations records, such as underreporting output or sales, to pay fewer taxes is unethical and illegal. Ethical operations keep accurate records and comply with tax and safety laws.

q: If a purchasing department orders materials late, what is the most likely effect on productivity?
o: The client's order will be delayed
e: Purchasing affects productivity directly: late materials stall production, delaying customer orders and wasting workers' time. Timely purchasing keeps operations running smoothly.

q: Companies that share information and plan together with their suppliers usually benefit from
o: reduced overall costs and smoother operations
e: Supply chain collaboration, like sharing forecasts, inventory data and plans, reduces stockouts, excess inventory and delays, lowering costs for everyone involved.

q: An ethical project manager assigns tasks and rewards based on merit, which means
e: Ethics in project management includes fair treatment: assigning work and recognition based on skills and performance, not friendship. Favoritism hurts morale and results.

q: Because the business field is very competitive, job seekers should
o: build skills and experience that set them apart
e: Competitive fields reward preparation. Developing skills, gaining experience through internships, DECA and volunteering, and networking help applicants stand out.

q: In a cover letter, the section that explains your relevant schooling and courses is the
e: A cover letter highlights qualifications that fit the job, including relevant education, experience and skills. It should be tailored to each position.

q: In some companies, employees with the most years of service get promoted first. This advancement pattern is based on
e: Seniority-based advancement rewards length of service. Many organizations also use merit, meaning performance and skills, or a mix of both. Seniority rewards loyalty and experience but may not always promote the strongest performer.

q: Following company protocols and policies helps employees
o: reinforce company values and work consistently
e: Policies reflect a company's values and keep work consistent, safe and fair. Following them builds trust with customers and coworkers and protects the company from legal and safety problems.

q: Companies with clear rules of conduct that employees follow usually
e: Clear rules of conduct set expectations for behavior, and when they're followed and enforced, misconduct declines. That protects the company's reputation and reduces legal risk.

q: Organizational goals that focus on improving customer satisfaction are examples of goals centered on the
e: Organizational goals can focus on profit, growth, employees or consumers. Goals about customer satisfaction center on the consumer and guide decisions on service and quality.

q: When the Federal Reserve lowers interest rates, businesses are most likely to
o: borrow more to expand, because loans are cheaper
e: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of borrowing, so businesses are more willing to take loans to buy equipment, hire and expand, and consumers borrow more for homes and cars. That extra spending stimulates the economy, which is why the Fed cuts rates when growth is weak.

q: A supervisor tells an employee, 'Your reports are accurate, but they're often a day late.' This feedback is useful mainly because it
o: lets the employee know how she's doing and what to improve
has no connection to her job
e: Good feedback tells you how you're doing and what's expected: here, keep the accuracy but improve timeliness. Specific, balanced feedback like this gives a clear target for growth, which is the main purpose of feedback at work.

q: A student chooses to work a Saturday shift for $120 instead of going to a concert. The concert is the student's
e: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative you give up when you make a choice. By choosing to work, the student gives up the concert, so the concert is the opportunity cost. A sunk cost is money already spent that can't be recovered, and fixed costs and marginal revenue are business terms that don't describe this trade-off.

q: Because a financial advisor's meeting is produced and used at the same moment, with the advisor present, services are described as
e: Services are inseparable: they are produced and consumed at the same time, usually with the provider present, like an advisor meeting or a haircut. Services are intangible, not tangible, and they are not durable goods. They also tend to be variable rather than standardized, because quality depends on who provides them and when.

q: The skills and knowledge a worker gains through education and training are called
e: Human capital is the knowledge, skill and experience that make a worker more productive, and it is built through education and training. Financial capital is money used to buy productive assets, capital goods are tools and equipment, and natural resources are part of land. Higher human capital tends to raise earnings, which is why education is treated as an investment.

q: A bank's mobile app lets customers transfer money at 2 a.m. on a holiday. The app mainly creates
e: Time utility is value created by making a product or service available when customers want it. Being able to transfer money at 2 a.m. on a holiday is about when, not where, so it is time utility. Form utility comes from changing a product's form, possession utility from making ownership easier, and place utility from availability where the customer is.

q: An auto dealer arranges a five-year loan so a buyer can drive home a new car today. The financing creates
e: Possession utility is value added by making it easier for a customer to own a product, most often through credit or financing. The loan lets the buyer take ownership today and pay over time. Form utility is about producing or changing the product, time utility is about when it is available, and information utility comes from providing knowledge such as labels or advice.

q: In which type of economic system does the government decide what is produced, how it is produced and what prices are charged?
e: In a command (planned) economy, the government makes the major economic decisions, including what to produce, how and at what prices. A market economy leaves these choices to buyers and sellers through supply and demand, a traditional economy relies on customs, and a mixed economy blends market decisions with some government involvement, as in the United States.

q: The United States is best described as a mixed economy because
o: markets make most decisions, but government regulates, taxes and provides some services
the government owns most businesses and sets most prices
customs passed down through generations decide what is produced
there is no government involvement in business
e: A mixed economy combines market decisions with government involvement. In the U.S., private buyers and sellers make most economic decisions, while government regulates industries, collects taxes, insures bank deposits through the FDIC and runs programs such as Social Security. Government ownership of most businesses describes a command economy, and customs describe a traditional one.

q: When a product's price is set below the equilibrium price, the market will most likely have a
e: At a price below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers are willing to supply, so the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied. That gap is a shortage, and it usually pushes the price up toward equilibrium. A surplus happens when the price is above equilibrium. The low price doesn't reduce demand; it raises the quantity demanded.

q: A lender charges a borrower with a low credit score a higher interest rate than a borrower with an excellent score. This shows that prices
o: reflect risk and ration scarce credit
are set by the government for all borrowers
are always the same for every customer
only cover a lender's fixed costs
e: Interest is the price of borrowing, and risk-based pricing uses that price to reflect the chance of default. A higher rate compensates the lender for the greater risk and rations credit toward borrowers most likely to repay. Rates are not set by the government for each borrower, they are not the same for everyone, and they cover expected losses and the cost of funds, not only fixed costs.

q: A market with only a few large firms, such as airlines or wireless carriers, that closely watch and react to each other's prices is a(n)
e: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large sellers whose decisions affect each other, so if one cuts prices, the others often match. A monopoly has a single seller, pure competition has many sellers of identical products, and monopolistic competition has many sellers of similar but differentiated products, like restaurants.

q: A homeowner can use the house as collateral for a loan because private enterprise protects
e: Private enterprise rests on property rights: the legal right to own, use and sell property. Because the owner legally owns the home and courts enforce that ownership, a lender can accept it as collateral and claim it if the loan isn't repaid. Price controls and government ownership are features of command systems, and private enterprise never guarantees profits.

q: In a private enterprise system, the profit motive mainly encourages businesses to
o: take risks, innovate and serve customers efficiently
let the government set their prices
e: The profit motive is the chance to earn a reward for taking business risk. It pushes owners to invest, innovate, control costs and meet customer needs better than rivals. Profit comes with the possibility of loss, so businesses don't avoid all risk. Government doesn't set most prices in private enterprise, and competitors don't share profits.

q: A company's sales rose 20%, but its profit fell. The most likely reason is that
o: its expenses grew faster than its revenue
e: Profit equals revenue minus expenses. If revenue grows 20% but expenses grow even faster, for example from higher ingredient costs or new staff, profit shrinks. The facts say revenue rose, so it didn't fall. A falling profit with rising sales means the margin shrank, not rose. High prices alone wouldn't explain rising sales with falling profit.

q: Which agency guarantees part of certain bank loans to small businesses, reducing the lender's risk?
e: The Small Business Administration guarantees a portion of loans such as its 7(a) loans, which go up to $5 million, so banks can lend to small businesses that might not qualify otherwise. The SEC regulates securities markets, the FDIC insures bank deposits, and the IRS collects taxes. None of those three guarantees small-business loans.

q: According to the SBA, small businesses make up about what share of all U.S. businesses?
e: The SBA Office of Advocacy's 2025 profile counted about 36.2 million small businesses, 99.9% of all U.S. businesses, employing about 45.9% of U.S. employees. This shows why small businesses matter so much to the economy: nearly every business is small, and together they employ almost half the private workforce.

q: When the government guarantees small-business loans or funds research to help industries grow, it is acting as a
e: Government plays several roles in business. When it guarantees loans, funds research or offers incentives, as the SBA and the CHIPS and Science Act do, it acts as a promoter that helps businesses grow. A regulator sets rules, a competitor would sell competing products, and when government buys goods and services it acts as a purchaser.

q: Negotiation between a labor union and an employer over wages, benefits and working conditions is called
e: Collective bargaining is the process in which a union negotiates with an employer on behalf of all its members, producing a labor contract. Arbitration is when a neutral third party makes a binding decision, mediation is when a neutral party helps both sides reach their own agreement, and a lockout is an employer keeping workers out during a dispute.

q: A state law that bans contracts requiring workers to pay union fees as a condition of employment is a
e: Right-to-work laws prohibit agreements that make paying union dues or fees a condition of keeping a job. The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947 allowed states to pass them, and 26 states had them after Michigan's repeal took effect in 2024. A closed shop, which required union membership before hiring, was banned by Taft-Hartley. Minimum wage laws set a pay floor and have nothing to do with union fees.

q: Compared with the private sector, the union membership rate among U.S. public-sector workers is
o: zero, because public workers can't join unions
e: In 2025, 32.9% of public-sector workers belonged to unions, compared with 5.9% of private-sector workers, according to the BLS (released February 2026). The overall rate was 10.0%. Public employees such as teachers, police and firefighters can join unions, and local government has the highest rate of all, 37.8%.

q: Labor productivity is measured as
e: Labor productivity is output divided by labor input, usually output per hour worked. Total hours, total wages and number of employees measure inputs or costs, not efficiency. A business raises productivity when it produces more with the same hours, often through better technology, training or processes. The BLS reported U.S. nonfarm productivity rose at a 3.6% annual rate in Q3 2026.

q: A bakery with one oven hires a fourth worker, who adds only 20 loaves a day while the second worker added 80. This illustrates
e: The law of diminishing returns says that adding more of one input, workers, to a fixed input, one oven, eventually adds less output per unit. The fourth worker adds far less than the second because workers are waiting for the oven. Economies of scale involve growing all inputs together over the long run, and the law of demand concerns prices and quantity demanded.

q: Real GDP differs from nominal GDP because real GDP
o: is measured in a foreign currency
e: Real GDP removes the effect of rising prices, so it shows whether the economy actually produced more. Nominal GDP uses current prices, so it can rise just because of inflation. Both measures include goods and services and count only final goods, to avoid double counting. U.S. GDP is measured in dollars.

q: During which phase of the business cycle do GDP and employment usually fall?
e: In a contraction, economic activity declines: GDP falls, unemployment rises and spending slows; a significant, lasting contraction is a recession. In an expansion, GDP and jobs grow. The peak is the high point before a downturn, and recovery is the rebound after the trough.

q: Which industry is most likely to be hurt in a recession because its sales swing strongly with the business cycle?
e: Cyclical industries, such as new cars, travel and home building, sell products people can delay, so their sales fall sharply in recessions. Defensive industries like groceries, utilities and prescription drugs sell necessities that people keep buying in any economy, so their sales stay steadier.

q: Which monthly government report measures total household spending on goods and services?
o: Personal consumption expenditures (PCE) from the BEA
The unemployment rate from the BLS
e: Personal consumption expenditures, published monthly by the Bureau of Economic Analysis, measure total household spending. Consumer spending makes up about 68% of U.S. GDP, which is why economists watch it closely. The unemployment rate measures joblessness, the producer price index measures wholesale prices, and the federal budget shows government spending.

q: If consumer spending rises 0.5% in a month but prices rise about the same amount, real consumer spending
e: Real spending adjusts for inflation. If households spent 0.5% more in dollars but prices also rose about 0.5%, they bought about the same amount of goods and services. That's what happened in September 2026: spending rose 0.5%, but real spending grew less than 0.1% (BEA). This is why economists focus on real, not nominal, spending.

q: A worker who quit one job and is looking for a better one is part of which type of unemployment?
e: Frictional unemployment is the short-term unemployment of people between jobs or entering the workforce, and it exists even in a healthy economy. Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs, cyclical unemployment is caused by recessions, and seasonal unemployment comes from jobs that end at certain times of year.

q: A retiree who isn't looking for work is counted in the unemployment rate as
e: The unemployment rate counts only people who are jobless and actively looking for work. Retirees, full-time students and others who aren't looking are outside the labor force, so they aren't counted as unemployed. That's why the unemployment rate (4.1% in October 2026, BLS) doesn't include everyone without a job.

q: Inflation caused by rising energy and raw material costs that push up businesses' prices is called
e: Cost-push inflation happens when production costs, such as energy, materials or wages, rise and businesses pass them on as higher prices. Gasoline topping $4.50 in spring 2026 is an example. Demand-pull inflation comes from spending growing faster than output, deflation is falling prices, and disinflation is prices rising more slowly.

q: Which borrower is usually helped by unexpected inflation?
o: A homeowner with a fixed-rate mortgage
A saver with cash in a checking account
A retiree living on a fixed pension
e: With a fixed-rate mortgage, the payment stays the same while inflation raises prices and usually wages, so the borrower repays with dollars that are worth less. Savers holding cash, retirees on fixed incomes and lenders receiving fixed payments are hurt, because inflation reduces the buying power of the money they hold or receive.

q: When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds usually
e: Bond prices move opposite to interest rates. When new bonds pay higher rates, older bonds with lower fixed payments are worth less, so their prices fall, and long-term bonds fall the most. This interest-rate risk contributed to Silicon Valley Bank's failure in 2023. Bond prices are never guaranteed before maturity.

q: The Community Reinvestment Act (1977) requires federally insured banks to
o: help meet the credit needs of their whole community, including low- and moderate-income areas
pay higher taxes than other businesses
offer free checking accounts to everyone
e: The Community Reinvestment Act encourages and requires federally insured banks to serve the credit needs of all the communities where they take deposits, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, and regulators rate their performance. It doesn't set special taxes, require free checking or limit lending to large corporations.

q: Customers, employees, suppliers, the community and shareholders who are affected by a company's decisions are its
e: Stakeholders are everyone affected by a business's actions. In 2019 the Business Roundtable, a group of major company CEOs, committed to serving all stakeholders rather than shareholders alone. Competitors are rivals, regulators are government agencies, and creditors are only one type of stakeholder.

q: Hiring, organizing work and controlling results so that the other activities of a business run well is the business activity of
e: Management plans, organizes, staffs, leads and controls a business so production, marketing and finance work together. Production creates the goods or services, marketing identifies customer wants and gets products to them, and finance obtains and manages the money the business needs.

q: A business that charges customers a recurring monthly fee for ongoing access to a service is using a
e: In a subscription model, customers pay a recurring fee, monthly or yearly, for continued access, as with streaming services or software. A freemium model gives basic features free and charges for upgrades, a franchise model sells the right to use a brand and system, and a razor-and-blade model sells a cheap base product and profits from refills.

q: A traditional bank earns most of its profit from
o: the spread between interest earned on loans and interest paid on deposits
e: A traditional bank's main business model is net interest income: it pays depositors one rate and lends money out at a higher rate, keeping the difference, plus fees. Advertising, membership fees and franchise royalties are other business models. Many fintechs, by contrast, earn mostly interchange fees from debit card use.

q: Fintech apps that earn most of their revenue from the small fee merchants pay each time a customer uses a debit card are relying on
e: Interchange fees are small percentages of each card purchase that merchants pay, part of which goes to the card issuer. Chime's 2025 IPO filing showed most of its revenue came from interchange fees, a different model from a traditional bank's reliance on loan interest. Overdraft fees and membership dues are other possible revenue sources, but they weren't the main model.

q: The number of employees a manager directly supervises is called the manager's
e: Span of control is the number of people who report directly to a manager. A wide span means a flatter organization with fewer layers; a narrow span means a taller one. The chain of command is the line of authority from top to bottom, line authority is the right to direct others, and an organizational chart is the diagram showing the structure.

q: Which tool scans a business's external environment by looking at political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors?
e: PESTLE analysis examines political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces outside a business that it can't control but must respond to. Break-even analysis finds the sales needed to cover costs, ratio analysis evaluates financial statements, and the payback period measures how long an investment takes to repay its cost.

q: An aging population that increases demand for retirement planning is an example of which type of factor in the business environment?
e: Population traits such as age, family structure and lifestyles are social factors. With more than 11,200 Americans a day turning 65 from 2024 through 2027, demand for retirement-income services is rising. Technological factors involve new tools, legal factors involve laws and regulations, and political factors involve government stability and policy.

q: An action that is legal but misleads customers in order to boost sales is best described as
o: unethical, because ethics go beyond what the law requires
a smart competitive strategy with no downside
e: Business ethics are moral principles such as honesty and fairness, and they set a higher bar than the law. A misleading tactic can be legal and still unethical. It also carries real business risk: Wells Fargo agreed to pay $3 billion in 2020 after sales pressure led employees to open accounts customers hadn't authorized.

q: A company that changes its main product or business model in response to a shifting market, like Netflix moving from DVDs to streaming, is making a
e: A pivot is a major change in a company's business model or main product to adapt to the market. Netflix pivoted from mailing DVDs to streaming and shipped its final DVD in 2023. A merger combines two companies, a recall pulls a defective product, and liquidation means selling off assets to close a business.

q: A bank sees that most customers now manage their accounts by app. The best way to adapt is to
o: improve its mobile app and turn low-traffic branches into advice centers
ignore the trend, since branches have always worked
e: Organizations adapt by responding to how customers now behave. In ABA's October 2026 survey, more customers named a mobile app as their top way to bank than any other method, and only about 10% preferred a branch. Improving the app meets that need, while converting quiet branches into advice centers keeps in-person help for big decisions and cuts costs.

q: A country should specialize in producing goods for which it has the lowest opportunity cost. This is the principle of
e: Comparative advantage means producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country. Even if one country is better at producing everything (absolute advantage), both countries gain by specializing in what they give up least to produce and then trading. Protectionism uses trade barriers, and a trade deficit is when imports exceed exports.

q: In September 2026 the U.S. imported more goods and services than it exported. This means the U.S. had a
e: The balance of trade equals exports minus imports. When imports exceed exports, a country has a trade deficit; in September 2026 the U.S. goods and services deficit was $105.0 billion (Census Bureau and BEA). A trade surplus is the opposite, and a budget surplus refers to government revenue exceeding spending, not trade.

q: A U.S. company moves production from China to Mexico to be closer to its customers and reduce shipping risk. This is called
e: Nearshoring means moving production to a nearby country, often to shorten supply chains and reduce risk. Offshoring means moving work to any foreign country, often far away for lower costs. Dumping is selling exports below their fair price, and moving production to Mexico has nothing to do with outsourcing to the government.

q: Which is a risk that globalization creates for businesses?
o: Long global supply chains can be disrupted by events far away
Businesses can sell only in their home country
e: Globalization connects businesses to suppliers and customers worldwide, which lowers costs and widens markets but also exposes them to disruptions anywhere along the chain, like chip shortages in 2021-22 or shipping detours around the Red Sea in 2023-24. Globalization gives customers more choices, opens foreign markets and increases foreign competition.

q: To reduce dependence on one country, Apple said a majority of iPhones sold in the U.S. in the June 2025 quarter came from India. This shows a company
e: By shifting production for the U.S. market from China to India, Apple spread its supply chain across countries to reduce tariff and concentration risk. It's still a global company importing from abroad, so it hasn't ended globalization or eliminated imports, and a company's sourcing decision has nothing to do with a country's economic system.

q: Which change would most likely strengthen the U.S. dollar against other currencies?
o: U.S. interest rates rising relative to other countries' rates
e: Higher interest rates attract foreign investors seeking better returns, which raises demand for dollars and strengthens the currency; in late 2026 expectations of higher U.S. rates helped push the dollar up. Higher inflation, political instability and falling rates tend to weaken a currency because they make holding it less attractive.

q: A strong U.S. dollar is generally good news for
o: Americans traveling abroad and businesses that import goods
U.S. companies' profits earned in euros
e: A strong dollar buys more foreign currency, so Americans traveling abroad and U.S. importers pay less for foreign goods and services. The same strength makes U.S. exports more expensive for foreign buyers, makes trips to the U.S. pricier for foreign tourists and shrinks the dollar value of profits earned in other currencies.

q: USMCA, the trade agreement among the United States, Mexico and Canada, replaced which agreement in 2020?
e: The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement took effect in 2020, replacing the North American Free Trade Agreement, which began in 1994. At its first joint review on July 1, 2026, the U.S. declined to renew it, triggering annual reviews, but the agreement remains in force. The EU, ASEAN and WTO are separate organizations.

q: An economic union of 27 countries with a single market, 21 of which share a common currency, is the
e: The European Union has 27 member countries and a single market for goods, services, people and money. Since Bulgaria adopted the euro on January 1, 2026, 21 EU members use the euro. ASEAN is a Southeast Asian bloc of 11 countries, Mercosur is a South American trade bloc, and USMCA covers the U.S., Mexico and Canada, none of which share a currency.

q: Which international organization sets global trade rules and settles trade disputes among its 166 members?
e: The World Trade Organization sets the rules of international trade and provides a system for settling disputes among member countries.
